title: Steve V. Wagner - Ozark Radio News
content: Steve V. Wagner, 67, of Willow Springs, Missouri, passed away peacefully on August 12, 2026, at his home surrounded by his family at his bedside. Steve was born on August 5, 1959, to William “Bill” and Glenna Wagner. He was a lifelong resident of the Willow Springs area and graduated from Willow Springs High school in 1978. Steve worked a variety of jobs before starting his career with Walmart in 1985. He remained with Walmart until his retirement in 2020. In 1999, Steve married the love of his life, Kathy, who was by his side throughout their life together. Their love and companionship were a special part of Steve’s life. Together they built a life filled with love, laughter, family, and countless memories. Their bond was a beautiful example of true love and devotion. A love that will continue to live on in the hearts of their family and all who knew them. Steve enjoyed the simple things in life. He loved deer hunting, riding four-wheelers, farming, and raising beef cattle. He also enjoyed good food, especially chocolate and Mtn Dew. Steve was known for his sense of humor and his ability to joke around with just about everyone he met. His laughter, personality, and friendship will be deeply missed by all who knew him. Steve’s faithful cat, Baby “21 years” was by his side through many years of love and companionship. She brought him joy, comfort, and unconditional love. Steve was preceded in death by his parents, William “Bill” and Glenna Wagner; his brother, Ted; sister-in-law, Cindy Wagner; and nephew, Travis. Steve is survived by his beloved wife, Kathy; his two sons, Mike (Marisa) Kelley and Timothy (Jenny) Starbuck. His grandchildren: Bayler, Camden, Brendan Kelley, Timothy, Steven, April, Lara, Landon, and Krystal Starbuck. His brother, Fred Wagner; three nieces, one nephew, and dear friends who loved him and will miss him dearly. Steve leaves behind a lifetime of memories for his family and friends. Steve lived a good life. One built on hard work, kindness, and love. He was a devoted husband, a proud father, a loving grandfather, and a true friend. He will be remembered for the way he could light up a room with his smile, the way he always had time for others, and the way he loved his family more than anything. Our hearts are heavy with his loss. His legacy of love, strength, and laughter will live on in all of us. Funeral services will be held Wednesday August 19, 2026, at Willow funeral home. Visitation will begin at 1:00 pm followed by the funeral service at 2:00 pm. Burial will follow at Nagle cemetery. Donations can be sent to Nagle cemetery. In loving memory of Steve V. Wagner a husband, father, grandfather, brother, friend, and one-of-a-kind jokester who will never be forgotten. Arrangements are under the direction of Willow Funeral Home, LLC.

title: SpaceX’s Starship generates more than twice the thrust of the Saturn V that carried humans to the Moon, yet after 13 test flights it still hasn’t demonstrated ship-to-ship refueling in orbit — one of the biggest technical hurdles standing between Starship and Mars - Space Daily
content:
Starship has unmatched liftoff thrust, but its Mars architecture still depends on an unproven vehicle-to-vehicle cryogenic refuelling system. By Mission Notes
·
Edited by
												Lachlan Brown SpaceX’s Starship V3 leaves its launch pad with roughly 18 million pounds of thrust. NASA credits the Saturn V with 7.6 million pounds at liftoff, meaning the current Starship stack produces well over twice the force of the rocket that dispatched Apollo astronauts towards the Moon. That comparison establishes Starship’s scale, not its readiness for Mars. SpaceX completed the vehicle’s 13th integrated test flight on 24 July 2026, but no two Starships have yet met in orbit, docked and passed propellant between them. That operation is central to the architecture because an upper stage consumes most of its launch load climbing away from Earth. One Starship did transfer liquid oxygen between two of its own tanks during Flight 3 in March 2024. NASA subsequently judged that experiment successful. It was an important fluid-management test, but it did not involve a tanker, a second ship, rendezvous hardware or a connection made in orbit. The distinction explains the apparent mismatch between the most powerful rocket ever flown and a fundamental capability that remains on its development list. Thrust gets a vehicle off the ground. A Mars campaign requires an entire transport system to work repeatedly after it gets there. NASA gives Saturn V’s launch thrust as 34.5 million newtons, equivalent to 7.6 million pounds-force. Five kerosene-burning F-1 engines powered its first stage. The rocket stood 111 metres tall and could place about 118 tonnes into Earth orbit. The Starship V3 flown on Flights 12 and 13 is about 124 metres tall. Its Super Heavy booster uses 33 methane-burning Raptor 3 engines, which together can generate approximately 18 million pounds-force at liftoff. Dividing 18 million by 7.6 million gives a ratio near 2.4. Thrust is force, however, not payload, reliability, efficiency or mission completion. It must exceed the vehicle’s weight to begin accelerating upwards, and extra thrust can lift a larger vehicle. It says nothing by itself about whether an upper stage can survive re-entry, fly again, support a crew for months or depart Earth orbit with enough propellant to reach another planet. Saturn V and Starship also embody different trades. Saturn V discarded three stages in sequence and sent only a relatively small spacecraft stack onwards to the Moon. Starship is designed to recover and rapidly reuse both its booster and upper stage. The reusable ship carries tanks, heat shielding, flaps and landing systems that an expendable lunar rocket did not have to bring home. The flight count begins with the first full Starship and Super Heavy launch in April 2023. It excludes earlier high-altitude ship prototypes, short hops, static firings and other ground tests. SpaceX’s launch listings identify Flight 13 on 24 July 2026 as the latest integrated test. Across that campaign, SpaceX has demonstrated hot-stage separation, controlled atmospheric entry, planned ocean splashdowns, in-space engine relights, payload deployment and catches of Super Heavy boosters with the launch tower. It has also lost vehicles, investigated failures and changed the design between generations. Flight 13 mattered because it gave the new V3 vehicle a substantially cleaner mission after Flight 12’s booster anomaly. The upper stage deployed 20 next-generation Starlink satellites, relit a Raptor engine in space and reached its planned Indian Ocean splashdown. Neither its flight plan nor any earlier one included rendezvous and transfer between two Starships. SpaceDaily’s preview of Flight 13 examined why engine relight mattered to NASA’s Artemis schedule. The completed test reduced that particular uncertainty. It did not erase the separate refuelling milestone. In March 2024, Starship Flight 3 carried an experiment backed by NASA’s Tipping Point programme. While coasting in space, the ship transferred approximately five tonnes of liquid oxygen from a smaller header tank into its main oxygen tank. The operation was designed to study large-scale cryogenic fluid behaviour in low gravity. NASA’s current TechPort record marks the project complete and says the demonstration achieved its milestone. That result matters because liquid does not simply remain pooled at the bottom of a tank in free fall. Before a transfer or engine burn, thrusters may need to settle it so pumps and lines receive liquid rather than vapour. The experiment also provided data about pressure control, subcooled oxygen and the conditions required to move cryogenic propellant. Yet the source tank, receiving tank and connecting plumbing were installed inside the same vehicle before launch. Nothing had to rendezvous or dock, and no coupling had to join two independently moving spacecraft. A full demonstration begins with two successful launches. A target Starship and a tanker must enter compatible orbits, navigate relative to each other, approach without collision and dock through a structural interface that can carry forces and fluids. Transfer lines exposed to space must be connected and chilled before extremely cold liquid methane and oxygen can flow through them. Both vehicles must control their orientation, settle propellant near tank outlets and maintain the pressure difference that drives transfer. Engineers must limit boil-off, avoid unstable two-phase flow and measure how much liquid actually reaches the receiving tanks. Doing this once is the first threshold. An operational mission would need the process to be routine and repeatable across several tanker launches on a tight schedule. A delay can leave stored propellant absorbing heat while the depot or mission ship waits in orbit. A March 2026 NASA Office of Inspector General report called large-scale vehicle-to-vehicle cryogenic transfer one of the most significant technical challenges facing SpaceX’s Human Landing System. It said a test once planned for March 2025 had slipped by a year and highlighted the additional risk of achieving the launch-pad turnaround needed for a refuelling campaign. The demonstration still had not occurred by the end of Flight 13. A rocket pays an enormous energy cost to reach low Earth orbit. Starship must lift its upper stage, payload, recovery equipment and propellant through the atmosphere and accelerate them to orbital speed. By the time the ship arrives, much of the propellant loaded on the ground has already been burned. For a high-capacity trip beyond Earth, SpaceX proposes launching tanker variants separately. They would deliver methane and oxygen to a depot or directly to the mission ship, allowing it to leave low Earth orbit with replenished tanks. The exact number of tanker launches depends on the evolving vehicle, payload, destination and how much propellant each flight can deliver. SpaceX’s published lunar architecture describes tanker Starships supplying an orbital depot before a lander fills up and continues to the Moon. Mars requires the same foundational capability to depart Earth with a large payload. A return mission introduces another challenge: producing methane and oxygen on Mars or delivering them in advance. Refuelling is therefore more than a way to improve payload performance. It is the bridge between Starship as a reusable launcher to low Earth orbit and Starship as the interplanetary transport SpaceX proposes. Saturn V happened to launch 13 times between 1967 and 1973. Its first two flights were uncrewed, its third carried Apollo 8 around the Moon, and later vehicles supported six lunar landings before the final Saturn V launched Skylab. The numerical symmetry with Starship’s 13 integrated flights is striking, but it is not a fair schedule comparison. Apollo’s rocket emerged from a vast government programme with extensive component, engine, stage and ground testing beyond the flights themselves. Saturn V was also designed for an expendable architecture whose stages did not have to return, dock with tankers or fly again. Starship’s test campaign is simultaneously developing propulsion, atmospheric return, tower recovery, payload operations and rapid reuse. SpaceX’s own 2026 prospectus names in-orbit propellant transfer and catching the upper stage among the key milestones still to be demonstrated. It also describes refuelling as the capability that would extend the upper stage into deep-space missions. Orbital transfer is not the only unfinished requirement for Mars. Starship still needs genuinely rapid reuse, a durable heat shield, high launch cadence, long-duration power and life support, radiation protection, reliable landing with heavy cargo and a credible path to return propellant. The Flight 13 result advances several nearer-term pieces without resolving that larger chain. Starship’s thrust advantage over Saturn V is real. So is the progress represented by 13 flights. The next transformation will not be another record at liftoff, but proving that separate reusable ships can repeatedly meet, dock and turn low Earth orbit into a filling station. title: Winnington, Elizabeth V. - McCrery & Harra
content:
Elizabeth V. Winnington, 80, of Garnet Valley, PA, died Wednesday, August 5, 2026, at her home surrounded by her family. A graduate of the University of Tennessee at Nashville and the University of Delaware, Beth worked as an Intensive Care Unit nurse and homemaker before finding her calling as a nurse paralegal for GEICO in Wilmington, Delaware. She was a committed member and Treasurer of Philanthropic Educational Organization (PEO), a non-profit organization providing scholarships, grants, awards, loans to women, especially those whose education has been interrupted and who find it necessary to return to school to complete a degree or certification. She was an avid reader and active member of two book clubs, one in her Belmont community and the other with her PEO sisters. She was also an active member of St. David’s Episcopal Church and its bible study group. She played an instrumental role in St. David’s outreach programs, including spearheading its support for Homeless Veterans and ensuring the success of its United Thank Offering. When not volunteering her time in support of her community, she enjoyed gardening and walking with each of her beloved dog companions through the years Beth was predeceased by her father Paul F. Winnington, her mother Elizabeth V. (Gibison), and siblings Frank Winnington and Mary Winnington. She is survived by her daughters Elizabeth Granda and Michele Granda (her spouse Karen Gausch); her grandson Nicholas Granda-Stone (his spouse Lauren Stone); her great-grandchildren Alden and Sullivan Granda-Stone; her sisters Jane Steele (Ray), Anne Marie Delle Donne (Bill) of Rehobeth, Meg Pryor (Jimmy), and Michele Winnington of Martha’s Vineyard, MA; and her brothers Paul Winnington Jr. (Lucille, deceased), Gerry Winnington (Nancy) of Dagsboro, and Peter Winnington (Barbara).She also leaves behind an innumerable number of cousins, nieces, nephews, and friends. A celebration of her life will be held at 10:00 on Saturday, August 22, 2026, am with a service at St. David’s Episcopal Church, 2320 Grubb Road, Wilmington, followed by a family attended interment in St. David’s adjoining Memorial Garden. In lieu of flowers, the family suggests donations be made to the Delaware Center for Homeless Veterans, 1200 N. title: Cadillac unveils V-ONE concept - AutoRacing1.com
content: Today, Cadillac revealed the V-ONE — a concept study combining the brand’s race-winning authenticity and bespoke Cadillac refinement. Its name unites the Cadillac V-Series performance legacy with a one-of-one, single-seat expression, the first of its kind for the brand. Rooted in performance engineering with shared Cadillac V-Series.R foundations, the V-ONE Concept explores how competition hardware can be translated into a driver-focused experience, while reinforcing Cadillac’s broader race-winning story across design, performance and technology. “The Cadillac V-ONE Concept is the ultimate manifestation of a customer performance concept and is a clear sign of our ambition for the Cadillac V-Series brand in the future,” said Dominic Najafi, Executive Design Director, Global Cadillac. The V-ONE is rooted in Cadillac’s LMDh racing program and informed by the V-Series.R race car, reinforcing that Cadillac performance is defined by real engineering rather than race-inspired styling alone. Co-developed by Cadillac Design, Cadillac Racing and chassis constructor Dallara, the concept is designed to deliver factory-level prototype performance and technology. Its story is backed by Cadillac Racing momentum in the IMSA WeatherTech Championship and the FIA World Endurance Championship, which together includes 10 wins, 16 pole positions and 32 podiums since the inception of the V-Series.R in 2023. That record includes the 2023 IMSA WeatherTech Championship manufacturer, team and driver titles, the 2025 Le Mans Hyperpole and Cadillac’s first 1–2 finish in the FIA World Endurance Championship at São Paulo. At the heart of the V-ONE is a V-8 hybrid powertrain that shares foundations with the Cadillac V-Series.R race car, underscoring the concept’s serious capability and authenticity. The concept also shares deeper race-bred architecture with the V-Series.R in areas such as suspension, transmission and select electronics. Even with that race-derived foundation, the V-ONE is intended to be easier to operate while maintaining a similar level of performance. The V-ONE’s exterior remains faithful to the dramatic proportions and visual intent of the V-Series.R race car, while introducing refined details that make the concept feel more advanced, more technical and more tailored to Cadillac luxury. Inside, the single-seat V-ONE Concept transforms pure prototype hardware into a fully bespoke, race-bred cockpit, blending exposed carbon structure with an immersive, custom UX/UI and deeply personalized materials to create an elevated expression of Cadillac performance luxury. The Cadillac V-ONE Concept will be on display at The Quail, A Motorsports Gathering in Carmel, California on August 14, 2026.

title: Big Ocean management comments on BTS V's hearing loss - Liam O'Dell
content: The 30-year-old, whose real name is Kim Tae-Hyung, shared information about his hearing during a livestream on Wednesday. According to BBC News, V said he has dealt with the issue for around two and a half years, and that his hearing worsened while he was serving in the military. V and his fellow group members Jung Kook; Jimin; Suga; RM; j-hope and Jin took part in mandatory military service, with BTS reuniting last year after the hiatus. The BBC reports V said: “If the hearing in my left ear is at 100, it’s only about 30 in my right.” V’s announcement makes him the latest K-pop star to share his experiences with hearing loss, after the trio Big Ocean (comprising deaf members Lee Chan-yeon, PJ and Kim Ji-seok) debuted in 2024. In a statement, its management Parastar Entertainment confirmed it had seen the news surrounding the BTS member. “It’s concerning to see hearing loss becoming more common, with stress and other factors potentially playing a role in many cases. “We don’t want to jump to any conclusions at this point, but we sincerely hope he takes good care of his health and hearing,” a spokesperson said. Liam’s debut non-fiction book, Selling Out the Spectrum, is a thorough, balanced deep dive into the issues surrounding the relationship between science and the autistic community, which explores how past damage can be effectively and meaningfully repaired. Search Results Koenigsegg's First V8 Client Gemera Breaks Cover at the Aurora Concours in Sweden Three years after Koenigsegg confirmed a V8-powered version of its four-seat Gemera, the first customer example has finally been showcased in public. The hypercar maker unveiled the car this weekend at the Aurora Concours in Båstad, Sweden, finished in a vivid Johan Röd paint over Engel Svart leather and Alcantara with red stitching accents. This particular client, Gemera, is equipped with the full Crystal Clear sound system, bespoke red-tinted Ghosts on the Aircore seats, and rides on Trofast Aircore carbon wheels.
The powertrain pairs a mid-mounted twin-turbocharged 5.0-liter hot V8 with Koenigsegg's Dark Matter electric motor via the brand's nine-speed Lightspeed Tourbillon Transmission (LSTT), a four-wheel torque-vectoring system that can send power independently to each wheel. Combined output is 2,300 horsepower, with a sub-2.0-second dash to 60 mph and a top speed in excess of 240 mph. The Gemera was the cover car in a feature we did last year on the most powerful production cars in the world.
<- Gallery ->
"Today is a big milestone for Koenigsegg, as we roll out the most technically advanced and most ambitious program in our history." - Christian von Koenigsegg, Founder, CEO, Koenigsegg
The Gemera realizes a dream von Koenigsegg has held for decades, a proper four-seat, high-performance supercar capable of seating four two-meter adults in comfort with room for luggage. The idea traces back to his childhood, when he first saw his friend's father's Lotus Excel.

Images: @Koenigsegg McLaren W1 First Drive: Ferocious Hypercar Transcends the Track You know things are getting serious when McLaren rolls-out the ‘1’ suffix. The origin story is, of course, the very first road car McLaren ever built, the F1. Designed by visionary Formula 1 aerodynamicist and engineer Gordon Murray, it arrived in 1992 and rendered all other supercars obsolete.

The tiny, lightweight F1 embraced carbon-fibre material technology, adopted a radical centre seat driving position with two passengers set back and either side and was powered by a 6.1-litre V12 engine from BMW that might as well have been passed down directly from the Gods. Game-changer? That doesn’t even come close to describing its impact, even if at the time sales didn’t come easy…
The P1 was very different. Rather than a unique side project from the Formula 1 team, it was instead a statement piece for McLaren Automotive, a new road car division still in its infancy. It arrived in 2013 and was a wild-eyed showstopper.

It traded the long-legged gait and supple suspension of the F1 for a weaponized hybrid system capable of delivering 903bhp and huge blue flames from its drainpipe exhaust. In Race mode, it lowered by 2-inches and its massive concave rear wing extended into the sky. The P1 was all about aerodynamic downforce, crazed acceleration and a snorting, angry soundtrack that mixed venomous twin-turbocharged V8 with the manic whirr of electric motors. Not so much a car as a force of nature.
And now there’s this: The W1. It’s a true successor to the P1 with a similar brief and, on the face of it, it evolves rather than radically reinvents McLaren’s vision for the ultimate hypercar. This is not a criticism. How could it be when the result is this dramatic and has such staggering, other-worldly potential?

The W1 has 1258bhp delivered to the rear wheels. It’s capable of 0-124 mph in 5.8-seconds, the quarter mile in 9.6-seconds at 167 mph and produces 2205lbs of downforce at 174 mph.
The active aerodynamics – particularly a rear wing that extends way out beyond the rear of the car – are pure performance art and deliver massive aerodynamic efficiency. The result, aside from looking extremely cool, is that the W1 is McLaren’s fastest road car around a racetrack. Ever. 

Their benchmark circuit is the breath-taking Handling Track at the Nardo proving ground in southern Italy, where the W1 beats their previous benchmark, the flyweight McLaren Senna, by three seconds per lap. Or “a lifetime” as they call it in racing. Maybe two lifetimes!
Core to the W1’s performance is the new ‘Aerocell’ carbon fibre tub. With integrated seats and a raised footwell to allow for inboard pushrod-operated front suspension – which in turn gives air a clean path to the huge underbody diffuser – it’s light, stiff, space efficient and has been instrumental in McLaren realising a full ground-effect concept. Just like last year’s F1 cars, which were the fastest ever made.

There is also an active front wing and the aforementioned complex rear wing dubbed ‘Active Long Tail’. All of which is very admirable. But the ‘anhedral’ or gullwing doors and the fantastically shirnked-wrapped feel to the minimalist, highly-focussed interior are a pretty good side effect. The W1 feels special.
Those fixed seats are perhaps a shade more upright than expected, and the driving position is less obviously racecar than, for example, the Aston Martin Valhalla or Ferrari F80. However, once you’ve adjusted the pedals (they move on a slider) and the delicate, slim-rimmed and alcantara-trimmed steering wheel, there’s an overwhelming sense of purpose.

The cabin is so tightly tailored and imparts a sense of lightness and agility before you so much as start the all-new 4.0-litre twin-turbocharged V8 engine, which makes 916bhp all on its own and revs to 9200rpm.
Reach up to a roof-mounted control panel to find the starter button. Maybe this fighter plane trope is a little corny, but somehow you feel thrilled rather than manipulated. The W1 has a sense of humour as well as all that motorsport-derived sophistication.

There’s a short delay, but when the engine does fire it’s instant – as the high-powered hybrid system negates the need for an old-school starter motor. A sharp flare of revs tells you that this engine is hyper-responsive and angry. On some deep level your brain and body have been sent all the signals required to prepare for something new and intense.
Ahead of us, an empty Mugello racetrack, so press and hold the blue button next to the red starter to select Race mode. The centre display graphic shows the W1’s transformation in real time as it lowers by 37mm at the front and 17mm at the rear whilst simultaneously undocking all that active aero goodness. 

Race mode is not road legal and is geo-locked. You can show your friends and neighbours the aero dance, but it won’t allow you to select a gear to actually drive unless you’re at a circuit. Incidentally, the rocker switches either side of the display binnacle allow further options now: Toggle up the Handling control on the left for Race+ (for F1-spec super smooth tracks) or stick to Race for gnarlier ones. 
On the right toggle select ‘GP’ for sustained performance over a stint or ‘Sprint’ to unleash all 1258bhp for a time attack. There’s also a DRS and Boost function on the steering wheel. But I guarantee you won’t have the mental capacity to use them…
Exit the pitlane, pin the throttle and W1 takes maybe a millisecond or two to gather its might (the gearing stretches to around 60mph in first, nearly 100mph in second, primarily to aid traction), but then lunges at the first turn with incredible ferocity.
It instantly feels light, almost like inertia is no longer a thing.

McLaren really does prize lightweight engineering, and at 3084lbs (dry) the W1 has a 278lbs advantage over the Ferrari F80. Plus, Ferrari uses figures for cars fitted with every single carbon fibre option. In reality, the gap is probably wider still.
The impression of agility and stunning control continues as the track is unravelled at startling pace. The electric motor mounted to the side of the new 8-speed dual-clutch transmission is good for 342bhp and 324lb ft and it boosts any low rev lethargy the new flat-plane crank V8 might have (spoiler alert: It doesn’t appear to have any), so the W1 just feels massively, almost impossibly powerful at any revs. Even so, there’s real reward for wringing it out to 9200rpm and the power curve feels superheated but organic, too.
In Race mode the steering – still hydraulically powered – has less assistance and it is noticeably heavier than other McLarens. However, that resistance is welcome as it gives you something to push against and imparts so much information about the front grip level. 
New Pirelli Trofeo RS tyres with a bigger front footprint than P1 or Senna really help. The front-end feels incredibly secure and the rear-axle follows with perfectly-aligned precision. The whole car feels super-stiff, completely locked into the surface and inspires confidence, but there’s an inherent agility and adjustability that means you’re quickly confident to push at its limits and really impose yourself on the chassis.
It’s such a complex car but the driving experience is intuitive, and the driver feels a key contributor rather than just amazed (or terrified) observer, holding on for dear life. Every dynamic ingredient really is shockingly effective and yet has a subtlety and lightness of touch. From that delicious steering to the incredible brakes, the W1 just feels so mission-focussed, so hooked-up. Only the new 8-speed gearbox is a slightly disappointment. It’s fast and punchy, but after the scintillating energy of the Ferrari F80 ’box it feels competent rather than inspired.
Other quibbles – it’s okay to quibble when the starting price is $2.1-million before tax and destination charge. Well, that new twin-turbocharged V8 sounds tightly wound and aggressive but if you have a P1 tucked in the garage you’ll miss the snorting, Darth Vader-style soundscape and all the drama that goes with it. Ferrari does this better, too. The F80 sounds deathly dull from the outside but is a riot of turbochargers, electric motors and all sorts of mechanical fury within the cockpit.
Even so, the W1 is wildly entertaining on track, and the rear-drive configuration makes it more of a challenge and more satisfying than the F80 when chasing lap times or just sliding around for fun. In the Ferrari, you must second-guess what the front e-axle might do, whereas in the W1 it’s all on you.
There are plenty of tools to help, including the ingenious Variable Drift Control, but somehow the W1 is more heroic. Or at least fools you into feeling more heroic – which is surely the point!

On the road? Nimble, loaded with feel and sublime response. The ride is noticeably tougher than, say, a 750S but the control is ramped-up too, and with a bit more speed the whole car finds a delicious rhythm.
Sport mode for the drivetrain brings some nice turbo whooshes and chirps, but the noise remains high-quality rather than extreme excitement. It is perhaps the one area the W1 feels just a little too tame.

Of course, there’s nothing tame about the raw performance… which is genuinely shocking and literally hurts your neck muscles after a few hours. How McLaren has given the W1 such immense traction through just two driven wheels is beyond me.
So, is it worthy of that ‘1’? I think so. Perhaps we won’t be talking about $25-million auction results for the W1 in 30 years from now, as we are for the F1.

Perhaps it doesn’t quite have the amazing presence and jaw-dropping star quality of the simply gorgeous P1. But it is such an intense experience and the way it marries stunning track performance with delicate poise and entertainment on normal roads is something akin to magic.
Maybe not ‘the one’ but definitely a searing, outrageous addition to McLaren’s fiercest family line. Just 399 W1’s will be built and they’re all sold. I’m not surprised at all.

The tiny, lightweight F1 embraced carbon-fibre material technology, adopted a radical centre seat driving position with two passengers set back and either side and was powered by a 6.1-litre V12 engine from BMW that might as well have been passed down directly from the Gods. Game-changer? That doesn’t even come close to describing its impact, even if at the time sales didn’t come easy…
The P1 was very different. Rather than a unique side project from the Formula 1 team, it was instead a statement piece for McLaren Automotive, a new road car division still in its infancy. It arrived in 2013 and was a wild-eyed showstopper.

It traded the long-legged gait and supple suspension of the F1 for a weaponized hybrid system capable of delivering 903bhp and huge blue flames from its drainpipe exhaust. In Race mode, it lowered by 2-inches and its massive concave rear wing extended into the sky. The P1 was all about aerodynamic downforce, crazed acceleration and a snorting, angry soundtrack that mixed venomous twin-turbocharged V8 with the manic whirr of electric motors. Not so much a car as a force of nature.
And now there’s this: The W1. It’s a true successor to the P1 with a similar brief and, on the face of it, it evolves rather than radically reinvents McLaren’s vision for the ultimate hypercar. This is not a criticism. How could it be when the result is this dramatic and has such staggering, other-worldly potential?

The W1 has 1258bhp delivered to the rear wheels. It’s capable of 0-124 mph in 5.8-seconds, the quarter mile in 9.6-seconds at 167 mph and produces 2205lbs of downforce at 174 mph.
The active aerodynamics – particularly a rear wing that extends way out beyond the rear of the car – are pure performance art and deliver massive aerodynamic efficiency. The result, aside from looking extremely cool, is that the W1 is McLaren’s fastest road car around a racetrack. Ever. 

Their benchmark circuit is the breath-taking Handling Track at the Nardo proving ground in southern Italy, where the W1 beats their previous benchmark, the flyweight McLaren Senna, by three seconds per lap. Or “a lifetime” as they call it in racing. Maybe two lifetimes!
Core to the W1’s performance is the new ‘Aerocell’ carbon fibre tub. With integrated seats and a raised footwell to allow for inboard pushrod-operated front suspension – which in turn gives air a clean path to the huge underbody diffuser – it’s light, stiff, space efficient and has been instrumental in McLaren realising a full ground-effect concept. Just like last year’s F1 cars, which were the fastest ever made.

There is also an active front wing and the aforementioned complex rear wing dubbed ‘Active Long Tail’. All of which is very admirable. But the ‘anhedral’ or gullwing doors and the fantastically shirnked-wrapped feel to the minimalist, highly-focussed interior are a pretty good side effect. The W1 feels special.
Those fixed seats are perhaps a shade more upright than expected, and the driving position is less obviously racecar than, for example, the Aston Martin Valhalla or Ferrari F80. However, once you’ve adjusted the pedals (they move on a slider) and the delicate, slim-rimmed and alcantara-trimmed steering wheel, there’s an overwhelming sense of purpose.

The cabin is so tightly tailored and imparts a sense of lightness and agility before you so much as start the all-new 4.0-litre twin-turbocharged V8 engine, which makes 916bhp all on its own and revs to 9200rpm.
Reach up to a roof-mounted control panel to find the starter button. Maybe this fighter plane trope is a little corny, but somehow you feel thrilled rather than manipulated. The W1 has a sense of humour as well as all that motorsport-derived sophistication.

There’s a short delay, but when the engine does fire it’s instant – as the high-powered hybrid system negates the need for an old-school starter motor. A sharp flare of revs tells you that this engine is hyper-responsive and angry. On some deep level your brain and body have been sent all the signals required to prepare for something new and intense.
Ahead of us, an empty Mugello racetrack, so press and hold the blue button next to the red starter to select Race mode. The centre display graphic shows the W1’s transformation in real time as it lowers by 37mm at the front and 17mm at the rear whilst simultaneously undocking all that active aero goodness. 

Race mode is not road legal and is geo-locked. You can show your friends and neighbours the aero dance, but it won’t allow you to select a gear to actually drive unless you’re at a circuit. Incidentally, the rocker switches either side of the display binnacle allow further options now: Toggle up the Handling control on the left for Race+ (for F1-spec super smooth tracks) or stick to Race for gnarlier ones. 
On the right toggle select ‘GP’ for sustained performance over a stint or ‘Sprint’ to unleash all 1258bhp for a time attack. There’s also a DRS and Boost function on the steering wheel. But I guarantee you won’t have the mental capacity to use them…
Exit the pitlane, pin the throttle and W1 takes maybe a millisecond or two to gather its might (the gearing stretches to around 60mph in first, nearly 100mph in second, primarily to aid traction), but then lunges at the first turn with incredible ferocity.
It instantly feels light, almost like inertia is no longer a thing.

McLaren really does prize lightweight engineering, and at 3084lbs (dry) the W1 has a 278lbs advantage over the Ferrari F80. Plus, Ferrari uses figures for cars fitted with every single carbon fibre option. In reality, the gap is probably wider still.
The impression of agility and stunning control continues as the track is unravelled at startling pace. The electric motor mounted to the side of the new 8-speed dual-clutch transmission is good for 342bhp and 324lb ft and it boosts any low rev lethargy the new flat-plane crank V8 might have (spoiler alert: It doesn’t appear to have any), so the W1 just feels massively, almost impossibly powerful at any revs. Even so, there’s real reward for wringing it out to 9200rpm and the power curve feels superheated but organic, too.
In Race mode the steering – still hydraulically powered – has less assistance and it is noticeably heavier than other McLarens. However, that resistance is welcome as it gives you something to push against and imparts so much information about the front grip level. 
New Pirelli Trofeo RS tyres with a bigger front footprint than P1 or Senna really help. The front-end feels incredibly secure and the rear-axle follows with perfectly-aligned precision. The whole car feels super-stiff, completely locked into the surface and inspires confidence, but there’s an inherent agility and adjustability that means you’re quickly confident to push at its limits and really impose yourself on the chassis.
It’s such a complex car but the driving experience is intuitive, and the driver feels a key contributor rather than just amazed (or terrified) observer, holding on for dear life. Every dynamic ingredient really is shockingly effective and yet has a subtlety and lightness of touch. From that delicious steering to the incredible brakes, the W1 just feels so mission-focussed, so hooked-up. Only the new 8-speed gearbox is a slightly disappointment. It’s fast and punchy, but after the scintillating energy of the Ferrari F80 ’box it feels competent rather than inspired.
Other quibbles – it’s okay to quibble when the starting price is $2.1-million before tax and destination charge. Well, that new twin-turbocharged V8 sounds tightly wound and aggressive but if you have a P1 tucked in the garage you’ll miss the snorting, Darth Vader-style soundscape and all the drama that goes with it. Ferrari does this better, too. The F80 sounds deathly dull from the outside but is a riot of turbochargers, electric motors and all sorts of mechanical fury within the cockpit.
Even so, the W1 is wildly entertaining on track, and the rear-drive configuration makes it more of a challenge and more satisfying than the F80 when chasing lap times or just sliding around for fun. In the Ferrari, you must second-guess what the front e-axle might do, whereas in the W1 it’s all on you.
There are plenty of tools to help, including the ingenious Variable Drift Control, but somehow the W1 is more heroic. Or at least fools you into feeling more heroic – which is surely the point!

On the road? Nimble, loaded with feel and sublime response. The ride is noticeably tougher than, say, a 750S but the control is ramped-up too, and with a bit more speed the whole car finds a delicious rhythm.
Sport mode for the drivetrain brings some nice turbo whooshes and chirps, but the noise remains high-quality rather than extreme excitement. It is perhaps the one area the W1 feels just a little too tame.

Of course, there’s nothing tame about the raw performance… which is genuinely shocking and literally hurts your neck muscles after a few hours. How McLaren has given the W1 such immense traction through just two driven wheels is beyond me.
So, is it worthy of that ‘1’? I think so. Perhaps we won’t be talking about $25-million auction results for the W1 in 30 years from now, as we are for the F1.

Perhaps it doesn’t quite have the amazing presence and jaw-dropping star quality of the simply gorgeous P1. But it is such an intense experience and the way it marries stunning track performance with delicate poise and entertainment on normal roads is something akin to magic.
Maybe not ‘the one’ but definitely a searing, outrageous addition to McLaren’s fiercest family line. Just 399 W1’s will be built and they’re all sold. I’m not surprised at all.

GALLERY-EMBED Search Results Koenigsegg's First V8 Client Gemera Breaks Cover at the Aurora Concours in Sweden Three years after Koenigsegg confirmed a V8-powered version of its four-seat Gemera, the first customer example has finally been showcased in public. The hypercar maker unveiled the car this weekend at the Aurora Concours in Båstad, Sweden, finished in a vivid Johan Röd paint over Engel Svart leather and Alcantara with red stitching accents. This particular client, Gemera, is equipped with the full Crystal Clear sound system, bespoke red-tinted Ghosts on the Aircore seats, and rides on Trofast Aircore carbon wheels.
The powertrain pairs a mid-mounted twin-turbocharged 5.0-liter hot V8 with Koenigsegg's Dark Matter electric motor via the brand's nine-speed Lightspeed Tourbillon Transmission (LSTT), a four-wheel torque-vectoring system that can send power independently to each wheel. Combined output is 2,300 horsepower, with a sub-2.0-second dash to 60 mph and a top speed in excess of 240 mph. The Gemera was the cover car in a feature we did last year on the most powerful production cars in the world.
<- Gallery ->
"Today is a big milestone for Koenigsegg, as we roll out the most technically advanced and most ambitious program in our history." - Christian von Koenigsegg, Founder, CEO, Koenigsegg
The Gemera realizes a dream von Koenigsegg has held for decades, a proper four-seat, high-performance supercar capable of seating four two-meter adults in comfort with room for luggage. The idea traces back to his childhood, when he first saw his friend's father's Lotus Excel. 
According to von Koenigsegg, the Gemera itself began taking shape in the mid-2000s, long before its eventual reveal. It first broke cover in 2020 with three electric motors and a tiny twin-turbo three-cylinder engine, and we’ve followed the story from its evolving design phase to its first driveable prototype testing phase in 2022.













View this post on Instagram























A post shared by Christian von Koenigsegg (@heycvk)


 
The production-spec hybrid version was revised in 2023 to employ Koenigsegg's single Dark Matter motor, lifting output to 1,400 horsepower, and news that the V8 variant was on the production line surfaced earlier this year in March.
Production of the Gemera is capped at 300 units, a ceiling set at the car's original 2020 unveiling. Koenigsegg has confirmed all 300 build slots are already accounted for. Original pricing started from $1.7 million, though the industry estimates have placed fully specified V8 examples well above $2 million.
For a company that has built its reputation on low-volume, two-seat hypercars, the four-seat Gemera represents a significant departure, one that doesn’t compromise on the brand’s core principles of high-performance speed and design details like the signature dihedral synchro-helix doors, now being offered in a more usable package as a Mega GT.

              Tyler Rampersaud   – August 14, 2026 The New Cadillac V-ONE Concept Previews A Possible Customer Racing Hyp Cadillac’s V-Series, the performance arm of the legendary American luxury manufacturer, has spent the past few years blossoming. Just over 20 years old, the V-Series started with performance versions of cars like the XLR convertible and the CTS and STS sedans, growing to include an iconic wagon, a powerful coupe, and other models over the years. This decade, the first V-Series SUV came in the form of a V-Series version of the legendary Escalade, and the V-Series also introduced an electric model with the Lyriq-V. Meanwhile, the nameplate gained an impressive racing presence with the V-Series.R, an LMDh hypercar that competes in the IMSA WeatherTech SportsCar Championship and the FIA World Endurance Championship, and an entry onto the Formula 1 grid this season. In both the IMSA and WEC series, the V-Series.R has earned impressive results in the endurance racing world, with 10 wins, 16 pole positions and 32 podiums for the car since it began racing in 2023. Its other achievements include the 2023 IMSA WeatherTech Championship manufacturer, team and driver titles, the 2025 Le Mans Hyperpole, and Cadillac’s first 1–2 finish in the FIA World Endurance Championship at São Paulo. 1 / 12 Now, a new concept, unveiled at The Quail, A Motorsports Gathering during Monterey Car Week, envisions an expansion of Cadillac’s racing hypercar presence, and it’s called the V-ONE. About the new V-ONE concept, Dominic Najafi, Executive Design Director at Global Cadillac (link opens in new tab/window), said, “The Cadillac V-ONE Concept is the ultimate manifestation of a customer performance concept and is a clear sign of our ambition for the Cadillac V-Series brand in the future.” It shares a foundation with the V-Series.R, and was created in collaboration with Dallara, the chassis manufacturer for the LMDh hypercar. However, the V-ONE’s V8 hybrid powertrain features a combined 830 horsepower, a significant increase from the regulation-restricted V-Series.R’s 671. Its aerodynamics are inspired by the V-Series.R, as well, and the two share suspension components, body proportions, and other details. Inside, the racing purpose of the car is maintained, with refined details that evoke Cadillac luxury, like an elegant interface and data visualization concept, a new wheel design, and a hand-sprayed gradient paintwork from silver to deep navy that nods to the grueling hours of endurance racing. The interior also features Cadillac Collection recycled fabrics, a serialized plaque on the door, and a seat that can be customized to driver specifications. While the new Cadillac V-ONE is a concept, other manufacturers in the endurance racing hypercar arena have created customer racing cars, like Ferrari’s 499P Modificata and the upcoming McLaren MCL-HY GTR, coming alongside the MCL-HY’s entrance to the endurance racing grid. With impressive success at the top class of endurance racing, Cadillac may be looking to expand its endurance hypercar presence to include customer racing with the new V-ONE. title: Meet the 830-HP Cadillac V-One Concept - autos.yahoo.com
content: Last year, Porsche built the 963 RSP for Roger Penske-after that, Cadillac apparently said, "we want a toke." Unveiled on the manicured lawns of The Quail during Monterey Car Week, the Cadillac V-One Concept is what happens when you yank an LMDh prototype race car out of the hauler, uncork the powertrain, and bolt in a bespoke leather-trimmed single seat inside. Its 830-horsepower, unrestricted hybrid powertrain makes the CT5-V Blackwing look like an airport shuttle. Because it doesn't have to play by IMSA or WEC Balance of Performance rules, the V-One throws the standard 670-horsepower LMDh power cap straight out the window. The underlying hardware remains pure prototype-anchored by a Dallara carbon-fiber monocoque, sprung with pushrod-actuated suspension, center-lock wheels, active aerodynamics, and massive underbody venturi tunnels that carry over virtually unchanged from the race car. "It's about as close to the race car as you can get," says Sean O'Shea, Cadillac LMDh Propulsion Manager GM's naturally aspirated LMC55R 5.5-liter DOHC V8 stays, but the hybrid electric setup-including a motor generator from Bosch and a Williams Advanced Engineering System battery-has been uncorked. "It takes 160 hours of build time just to assemble the engine," adds O'Shea. "It's all done in Pontiac, Michigan by people that have built race engines their whole careers. They're hand-picked for the job." Total system output has been juiced to 830 combined horsepower, all sent straight to the rear tires via an Xtrac seven-speed sequential gearbox. "You get on the straightaway, hit a button and get an extra 134 horsepower," O'Shea explains. "I couldn't even imagine that. These things are already so fast, adding a bunch more power with the press of a button is incredible." Cadillac won't explicitly say the car is street legal, but there seem to be clues. Inside the cockpit, the typical barren race controls get swapped for soft Cadillac Collection fabrics, a custom digital user interface display, a yoke-style steering wheel, and tailored switchgear to the individual owner. There's even a little shelf with an integrated strap to hold your helmet in place as you travel to the race track. "The interior of the car is one of the main selling points with the car," said O'Shea. "You open the doors and you look inside and it's a clean, purpose-built race car with a bespoke Cadillac interior." Outside, a gradient paint scheme shifts from bright silver at the nose to deep navy blue at the tail-a nod to the day-to-night transition during 24-hour endurance races. A small serialized door plaque hints that Cadillac plans to build more than just once. The automaker certainly missed a trick through, the Porsche has a cup holder. Become an AutoGuide insider. title: Our Take on the Likely Outcome of the NAW v. Feldon Litigation Challenging Oregon's EPR Program. - JD Supra
content:
Now that the trial is over for National Association of Wholesaler-Distributors (“NAW”) v. Feldon, a case challenging Oregon’s landmark Plastic Pollution and Recycling Modernization Act (“RMA”) in the U.S. District Court for the District of Oregon, many of us are waiting with bated breath for the final decision — and speculating on the outcome. Based on the court's supplemental briefing requests, we are predicting that the court is unlikely to invalidate the basic architecture of the program. More likely, the court may target the exemption for Oregon public bodies — or the court could enjoin the Oregon Department of Environmental Quality (“DEQ”) from approving the Program Plan submitted by the producer responsibility organization (“PRO”) to DEQ unless the Plan provides for greater transparency and/or participation in setting fees. The plaintiffs in NAW v. Feldon assert constitutional challenges to Oregon’s extended producer responsibility (“EPR”) program and have also brought or joined similar challenges to Colorado's and California's EPR programs. Unlike claims that turn on Oregon-specific statutory language, the Dormant Commerce Clause claims in NAW v. Feldon attack the fundamental structure common to other state EPR programs — a single state-selected PRO funded through interstate producer fees — whereas the Due Process claims generally single out specific features (some of which are unique to Oregon’s program). After trial, the court asked for a number of supplemental briefings related to the Due Process Clause but did not request any additional briefing on the Dormant Commerce Clause, leading some to speculate that the court had already decided the Dormant Commerce Clause issues in the plaintiffs' favor but was not convinced by the Due Process Clause challenges. On August 6, 2026, however, Judge Simon asked for one more round of supplemental briefing — specifically, whether the RMA's exemption for certain Oregon public bodies that qualify as “small producers” is facially discriminatory under the Dormant Commerce Clause. A judge planning to strike down the program under a broad Dormant Commerce Clause challenge would have little reason to drill into one narrow issue. Meanwhile, the court’s earlier requests for supplemental briefings about the Due Process Clause signaled that the court has concerns that the case is not ripe and/or that the court could not fashion a remedy for some of the alleged constitutional deficiencies — particularly as to provisions in the producer agreements with the PRO (e.g., the arbitration clause) because the PRO is not a party in the litigation. The court, however, would presumably have authority to enjoin the DEQ from approving the PRO’s Program Plan to the extent the PRO adopted measures that the court deemed unconstitutional — such as the lack of transparency in setting fees. In the supplemental briefing recently requested by the court, the plaintiffs have argued that any constitutional deficiency — such as the exemption for Oregon public bodies — is sufficient to overturn the entire EPR program. In a response requested by the court and filed this week, the DEQ claims that invalidating the entire program based on the unconstitutionality of a single provision would be an abuse of discretion, citing the Oregon law on severability, which allows displacement only if the statute says otherwise, the valid and invalid parts are inseparably interdependent, or the remainder can't function without the invalid part. ORS 174.040. Whatever the outcome, this case will be a bellwether for EPR programs nationally, as pending challenges to other states' programs raise many of the same claims. That said, other state challenges also raise different claims (e.g., First Amendment challenges) and different statutory schemes, meaning even after a final decision in NAW v. Feldon, the disposition of litigation in other states remains an open question.  Stay tuned for our analysis once the court rules. title: Cadillac V-One concept: a real Le Mans pedigree at last - AutoNext.co
content: Concept cars love to borrow the language of the track. Press releases are thick with phrases like race-bred and motorsport-derived, and almost all of them are marketing, a costume draped over a design study that has never turned a wheel in anger. Cadillac's new V-One concept, revealed at The Quail during Monterey Car Week, is the unusual one where that language is literally true. It is a single-seat, track-only machine that shares real suspension hardware with the Cadillac that races at Le Mans, and it is aimed at lapping within 10% of that car. For a brand that spent two decades borrowing a performance image it had not yet earned, the V-One is the moment the receipts finally arrived. Underneath the drama sits a naturally aspirated 5.5-litre hybrid V8 producing a combined 842 hp, the figure Cadillac quotes as 830 horsepower, with roughly 136 hp of that delivered instantly by an electric motor as a stab of extra thrust on demand. It drives through a seven-speed sequential gearbox and a small hybrid battery, and it is a single-seater: one central seat, no passenger, no compromises toward everyday use. The suspension is not merely inspired by the race car, it is shared with it, double wishbones front and rear, pushrod-actuated coil and torsion springs, and separate lateral and heave dampers, the same architecture that survives twenty-four hours at Le Mans. The bodywork wears a hand-sprayed gradient that fades from silver to deep navy, a nod to a race that runs from daylight into darkness. Cadillac has not announced a price or confirmed production, so treat it as a concept, not an order form. This is the detail that makes the V-One more than another rich concept. For most of the V-Series era, Cadillac built fast road cars and then reached for a racing story to justify the badge, borrowing prestige from a motorsport record that was thin. The V-One reverses the flow entirely. Here the racing came first and the concept borrows from it, taking the hardware of a proven endurance winner and building a road-brand halo around it. That only works because the record is now real: Cadillac swept the 2023 IMSA WeatherTech titles, took Hyperpole at Le Mans in 2025, and scored its first one-two finish in the World Endurance Championship. The V badge is no longer a promise. It is, for the first time, a description. Just as telling is what Cadillac chose not to do. The V-One is not a road-going hypercar chasing a headline power figure, and it is pointedly not a rival to the Corvette. It is a single-seat, track-only object with one honest job: to get as close as a customer machine can to the pace of the actual race car. That restraint is unusual and welcome. Rather than another road hypercar promising a race pedigree it cannot back up on a Tuesday, Cadillac built the one thing its motorsport results genuinely license it to build. It is the same logic that lets Toyota turn a GT3 programme into a road-and-track supercar, or Lamborghini bank credibility from a first IMSA win: earn it on track, then spend it. It is easy to file this under American brand, American toy, and move on, but the V-One is aimed squarely at exactly this audience. Cadillac earned every one of these credentials in Europe, at Le Mans and across the endurance calendar, and it is spending them at the moment it is trying hardest to be taken seriously here, bringing bespoke Escalades and the Cadillac name to European buyers and preparing a full works entry into Formula 1. A halo car exists to change how a badge feels, and Cadillac needs that shift most in the one market that has always been coolest toward it. The V-One is a concept, but it is also a pitch, aimed at Europe in Europe's own language of racing. The lazy read of the V-One is that Cadillac has finally built a proper halo car. The sharper read is that it has finally built one it is allowed to. For twenty years the V-Series traded on an image of speed that the track record could not quite support, and everyone politely pretended not to notice. What changed is not the styling or the marketing budget; it is that Cadillac went to Le Mans, did the unglamorous work of endurance racing, and won. The V-One is simply the first car honest enough to be built the right way round, from the race car outward. So the number worth remembering is not 842 hp. It is the pledge to lap within 10% of the actual competition car, because that is a claim Cadillac can be measured against rather than one it can only assert. When a concept invites you to check its homework instead of asking you to take its word, the pedigree has stopped being a costume. That is the real news here, and it is why the V-One matters more than a single-seat track toy for a handful of collectors ever should. Set AutoNext as your preferred source on Google Discover Cadillac has launched Curated by Cadillac, a bespoke personalisation programme, on the electric Escalade IQ, and the option alone costs 54,995 dollars. It brings the hand-built Celestiq experience, 160 hand-applied paints, 44 interior configurations and a design concierge, to a wider audience, built at the same Michigan Artisan Center. The programme is North America only for now, which raises the obvious question for a brand pushing hard into Europe: when does the continent get it? Cadillac has removed Graeme Lowdon as its Formula 1 team principal months into the team's debut season, replacing him with F1 veteran Marcin Budkowski in a decision the outgoing boss reportedly learned of only hours before it became public. Toyota Gazoo Racing's GR GT, described as the spiritual successor to the Lexus LFA, arrives in 2027 as a standard road car and a more aggressive track variant. The standard car pairs a 4.0-liter twin-turbo hybrid V8 with 650 hp, while the hotter version has already been spotted testing at the Nurburgring against a Porsche 911 GT3 RS, before the base model has reached a single customer.

title: At the Bar of Four Seasons Hotel George V, Paris Thibault Méquignon Writes a New Chapter in Parisian Mixology - Four Seasons Press Room
content: FS News brings you the latest news and info, straight to your inbox. That email address has already subscribed. You may enter a different email address below. Having shaped his eye and sensibility for the cocktail in London, New York, Paris, and Dubai, Thibault Méquignon joins the Four Seasons Hotel George V, Paris with one ambition: to establish the Bar as a destination in its own right. Nourished by gastronomy and guided by emotion, his vision goes beyond simple cocktail creation to imagine an experience where taste, hospitality, and atmosphere respond to one another, with complete "simplexity." Simplexity, or the Art of Turning Complexity into the Obvious For Thibault Méquignon, the most accomplished creations are often those whose sophistication disappears behind the emotion they evoke. He sums up this approach in one word: "simplexity" — the art of making simple what is, in reality, the result of long and meticulous work. Behind the apparent obviousness of a cocktail lie hours of research, extraction, infusion, and concentration. The technique exists, but it must never take precedence over the experience. In this era of quiet luxury, this philosophy aligns with a new conception of luxury — one grounded more in precision, sensitivity, and personalization than in display. It was in the kitchens of Alexandre Gauthier, at La Grenouillère, that Thibault Méquignon forged his first relationship with taste: one rooted in product, precision, and creative instinct. Before turning to mixology, he developed a deeply gastronomic approach there, which he now carries behind the bar, conceiving each cocktail not from a spirit, but from a gustatory emotion. His creations are born from a pairing of flavours, a texture, a sensation, or a memory, recorded in the personal notebooks he carries everywhere, before being refined in the lab. He then searches for the spirit best able to express that original emotion with the greatest precision. The Bar at Four Seasons Hotel George V, Paris: Reimagining the Experience Beyond the Cocktail His arrival at the palace on Avenue George V is part of a broader ambition: to make the Bar a destination in its own right. While palace hotels have long treated the bar as a natural extension of the lobby or the dining offering, Four Seasons Hotel George V, Paris now asserts a different vision — that of a space with its own identity, conceived as a self-contained world, orchestrated down to the smallest detail. This transformation rests on several pillars: evolving service standards, rethinking production protocols, a new approach to cocktail creation, and in-depth work on the atmosphere of the space itself. For Thibault Méquignon, the cocktail is only part of the experience: light, music, and the rhythm of the evening all play a role in the story being told. As the hours pass, the atmosphere evolves: the lighting dims, curtains open or close, the tempo shifts. Nothing is left to chance, yet nothing feels staged. This new identity is also reflected in the menus. Alongside the great classics of French heritage served at Le Cinq and L'Orangerie — the Bloody Mary, the Boulevardier, the French Martini — Thibault Méquignon has created a collection of twelve signature cocktails for the Bar, inspired by travel, memory, and sensation. His creations do not tell the story of destinations — they capture their traces. From spices discovered in South Indonesia to teas brought back from Japan, from floral notes to more comforting accords inspired by pastry, each cocktail becomes a personal interpretation of taste — an approach that naturally converses with the kitchens of Four Seasons Hotel George V, Paris, building bridges between cocktail and gastronomy. "Only sustained work on a cocktail allows a flavour to be pushed this far," says Thibault Méquignon. Thibault Méquignon continues today to pursue this rare balance: making complexity disappear behind the obvious, to offer an experience where every detail matters. His ambition can be summed up in a few words: to create cocktails that awaken the senses, summon memory, and leave a lasting impression — an approach in which technique fades behind emotion, and where every detail, from creation to service, including light and music, transforms a moment at the bar into a memorable experience. This approach can be seen in creations such as Beurre Noisette, where vanilla-infused gin meets the warm, lightly toasted roundness of brown butter, extended by the freshness of lime — a composition that evokes the childhood memory of lemon meringue tart. With Bee Pollen, he explores another sensory register: cognac opens onto the gentle bitterness of bee pollen, lifted by the vivacity of verjus and the floral delicacy of chamomile. As for L'Oseille, it plays on the contrast between vegetal acidity, the milky freshness of a lassi, and the camphorous notes of green cardamom. Three creations that illustrate his way of transforming an emotion, a memory, or a pairing of flavours into a sensory experience. "I want taste buds to widen and eyes to light up with wonder," says Méquignon. Behind this creative freedom lies an absolute mastery of the fundamentals. Thibault Méquignon executes the great classics of mixology with the same demand for precision and balance, convinced that all innovation is first built on a perfect knowledge of the basics. Originally from Wimereux, a small seaside town on the Côte d'Opale, Thibault Méquignon grew up between the seascapes of northern France and a particular attentiveness to product. After a marketing baccalaureate, he chose to redirect his path toward hospitality and enrolled at the hotel school in Le Touquet, before training, through a work-study program, in the kitchens of Alexandre Gauthier at La Grenouillère. This first experience proved formative. Amid the marshlands, in close contact with the chef, market gardeners, and producers, he discovered a sensitive approach to cooking — one rooted in respect for the product, precision in pairing, and creativity as a language. After a period in the kitchen, he asked to move to the dining room to explore another facet of hospitality: that of encounter, dialogue, and the sharing of taste. His discovery of bartending came almost by chance: one evening, he stepped in to help a friend behind the bar of his establishment in Boulogne-sur-Mer. The experience was a revelation. There, he rediscovered what had drawn him to gastronomy: working with flavors, precision of gesture, and above all, direct exchange with guests. After earning a complementary bartending certification at the school in Talence, followed by experience at the Grand Hôtel de Bordeaux, he decided to cross the Channel to join the Experimental Cocktail Club in London, then regarded as one of the birthplaces of cocktail culture. Between 2012 and 2015, he perfected his English, discovered the codes of a thriving international scene, and gradually rose through the ranks to become assistant bar manager. It was during an evening at the Experimental Cocktail Club that he met Nico de Soto — a defining encounter. The two men shared the same vision of the craft, and a few months later, as the French bartender prepared to open Mace in New York, he invited him to join the venture. A few years later, Nico de Soto called on him again for the opening of a new address in Paris: Danico, which he founded in 2016 with Julien Ross and Alexandre Giesbert in the heart of the Galerie Vivienne. At just 25 years old, Thibault Méquignon took the helm behind the bar as head bartender. This experience confirmed his creative, precise, and deeply taste-driven approach to the cocktail, and propelled him onto the international stage. In 2021, he moved to Dubai, a rising powerhouse of global hospitality, where he took charge of the bars at the Burj Al Arab within the Jumeirah group, before becoming Head of Beverage for One&Only. Leading a team of 75 bartenders and working alongside world-renowned chefs, he deepened a global vision of the craft, at the crossroads of gastronomy, service, and creation. After a consulting mission with the LVMH group, during which he notably designed cocktail offerings for international addresses, he returned to Paris with a new challenge: to write a new chapter for the Bar at Four Seasons Hotel George V, Paris. title: Cadillac Reveals V-ONE Concept Based on V-Series.R LMDh Car - Sportscar365
content: Cadillac takes wraps off concept prototype based on V-Series.R LMDh car… Cadillac has taken the wraps off its V-ONE prototype, billed as a concept study that “unites the Cadillac V-Series performance legacy with a one-of-one, single-seat expression” marking the first of its kind for the brand. Based on the Dallara-chassied V-Series.R LMDh car that competes in both the FIA World Endurance Championship and IMSA WeatherTech SportsCar Championship, the V-ONE Concept was unveiled Friday at The Quail, A Motorsports Gathering in Carmel, Calif., as part of Monterey Car Week. “The Cadillac V-ONE Concept is the ultimate manifestation of a customer performance concept and is a clear sign of our ambition for the Cadillac V-Series brand in the future,” said Dominic Najafi, Executive Design Director, Global Cadillac. The concept car, co-developed by Cadillac Design, Cadillac Racing and Dallara, is designed to deliver factory-level prototype performance and technology. The V8 hybrid powertrain shares foundations with the V-Series.R, but can produce an increased combined 830 horsepower, along with “race-bred” suspension, transmission and selected electronics from the LMDh car. Among other shared components include double wishbone suspension, pushrod-actuated coil and torsion spring elements with lateral and heave dampers on the front and rear. Additionally, the V-ONE Concept features an “intuitive, race-inspired interface and data visualization concept that gives drivers clear feedback and coaching as they explore the car’s full capability.” Cadillac has not made any indications of it plans to build and offer the car to customers, in what would most likely be for a track-day setting, similar to the Ferrari 499P Modificata and McLaren’s MCL-HY GTR. After building his reputation with the greatest chefs and establishing his own voice in Bordeaux, chef Bertrand Noeureuil opens a new chapter of his career at the Four Seasons Hotel George V, Paris. Appointed chef of L'Orangerie, he will also be tasked with breathing new culinary identity into the Bar, La Galerie, and the hotel's Room Service. Crowned Talent of the Year 2026 by La Liste, he embodies the emergence of a singular voice in French gastronomy, driven by a cuisine in dialogue with the living world. Beyond seasonality, which for him is simply self-evident, chef Bertrand Noeureuil envisions a cuisine of correspondences: a sensitive form of writing through which the chef does not seek to impose his vision on nature, but rather to listen to it, to understand its rhythms, and to reveal the invisible connections between a product, a season, a gesture, and an emotion. For chef Bertrand Noeureuil, culinary creation is not about imposing a vision on nature, but about revealing what it already holds within itself. The chef thus becomes a conduit for the living world: one who observes, connects, and brings to light correspondences that are often invisible, yet feel entirely self-evident. The ripeness of a vegetable calls for a particular cooking method; the humidity of a season suggests a texture; the freshness of spring invites vegetal notes; the depth of autumn calls for richer, more complex jus. Each season thus has its own vocabulary. Winter inspires slow cooking, creamy sauces, veloutés, and sabayons. Spring brings forth herb coulis and more vegetal expressions. Summer favors immediacy and freshness, with raw preparations or wood-fire cooking. Autumn reveals roasting jus, broths, and deeper sauces. Season, then, is no longer a mere calendar marker — it becomes a culinary grammar. Beneath the glass roof designed by Pierre-Yves Rochon, L'Orangerie offers a setting in constant transformation, where light, vegetation, and the seasons reshape the perception of the space every day. This architecture naturally resonates with chef Bertrand Noeureuil's cuisine: a cuisine conceived in harmony with its environment. The restaurant will offer four menus a year, each one a chapter in a seasonal collection. Each day, the available produce will be noted on a handwritten sheet at the opening of the menu, giving the kitchen the flexibility needed to stay closely attuned to the rhythm of nature. The menu will therefore not be built around a fixed list of ingredients, but around culinary gestures: braising, roasting, grilling, infusing, extracting. As the produce evolves, the intention remains constant. Like a natural ecosystem, a restaurant only finds its harmony through the precise interplay between each of its contributors. The creations of Michaël Bartocetti, Executive Pastry Chef of the Four Seasons Hotel George V, Paris, will thus naturally converse with Bertrand Noeureuil's cuisine. Sharing the same attentiveness to produce, seasons, and the balance of flavors, together they will compose a piece in which dessert does not conclude the meal, but extends its narrative. Already alongside the chef at L'Observatoire du Gabriel, Elsa Jeanvoine, restaurant director and Meilleur Ouvrier de France in service and table arts, will bring this philosophy to life in the dining room. Finally, this pursuit of resonance will continue in the glass. Under the direction of David Piquet, Head Sommelier of Le Cinq and L'Orangerie, the sommeliers will craft food and wine pairings in harmony with the chef's creations, while Thibault Méquignon will offer a complementary reading at the Bar, through food and cocktail pairings that evolve with the seasons. Born in Toulouse, Bertrand Noeureuil grew up between city and countryside, where memories of his maternal grandparents' family farm shaped his connection to the living world from an early age. Yet cooking was not an obvious path. Coming from a family with no ties to the culinary world, he first developed a passion for design and interior decoration, drawn to composition, materials, and the balances specific to the applied arts. This sensibility would find a new outlet in gastronomy: the plate becomes a space for creation where every element converses with the whole. This connection to the living world, paired with his aesthete's eye, would become the two pillars of his culinary identity, guided by material, gesture, and the singularity of each product. Learning from the Masters: Between Rigor and Intuition After his initial training in the Toulouse region, Bertrand Noeureuil joined the great houses of French gastronomy, where he refined his technique and gradually shaped his culinary language. Alongside Yannick Alléno, at Le Meurice and later at 1947 in Courchevel, he developed an approach grounded in research, precision, and the concentration of flavours. His summer experiences with Arnaud Donckele, at La Vague d'Or in Saint-Tropez and later during the opening of Plénitude at Cheval Blanc Paris, opened another path: an intuitive, abundant, and sensitive cuisine, where taste, texture, and color come together as a true language. From these two mentors, he retains two complementary legacies: rigor and precision of technique on one hand; instinct, storytelling, and the emotional power of flavour on the other. In Bordeaux, at the helm of L'Observatoire du Gabriel, he wrote the first pages of his personal cuisine. Rooted in the Aquitaine region, nourished by direct relationships with producers and close observation of the seasons, it asserts a singular signature. Awarded two Michelin stars in just eighteen months, it reveals his defining hallmarks: precision in cooking, the importance of sauces, acidity as a line of tension, and a balance between bold flavors and lightness of execution. A New Chapter for the Gastronomy of the Four Seasons Hotel George V, Paris At L'Orangerie, chef Bertrand Noeureuil will offer two menus, in six and nine courses — to be leafed through like precious booklets, to be kept as testaments to a particular cycle. While the six-course version will reveal the essence of the season, the nine-course journey will offer a broader expression through two interpretations: one marine and vegetal, the other featuring a meat selected according to the season, with game as autumn's natural expression. This vision will also extend to La Galerie, the Bar, and Room Service, where the chef will guide the evolution of these experiences in keeping with his culinary identity. Alongside chefs Christian Le Squer, Simone Zanoni, and Michaël Bartocetti, chef Bertrand Noeureuil thus helps write a new chapter in the gastronomic history of the Four Seasons Hotel George V, Paris, carried by its six Michelin stars and an unwavering ambition for precision, creativity, and emotion. title: Cadillac V-One Turns Its Le Mans Racer Into an 830-HP Track Toy - autos.yahoo.com
content: The Cadillac V-One Concept, unveiled during Monterey Car Week, is a single-seat track car that draws directly from the V-Series.R prototype Cadillac races in both the IMSA WeatherTech SportsCar Championship and FIA World Endurance Championship. While Cadillac is calling the V-One a concept for now, the exercise suggests the automaker is looking at offering it to its wealthy customers, giving them, in essence, a factory-built track car with performance approaching that of its competition machinery. The V-One was developed jointly by Cadillac Design, Cadillac Racing, and Dallara, which builds the chassis for the V-Series.R. And it goes way beyond just replicating the race car's look; the concept actually shares significant hardware with it, including elements of its suspension, transmission, electronics, and hybrid powertrain. That powertrain combines a V8 engine with hybrid assistance to produce 830 hp. Cadillac hasn't released detailed performance figures, but the automaker says the V-One is intended to deliver performance comparable to the V-Series.R while being easier for a nonprofessional driver to operate. The suspension echoes the race car's double-wishbone layout, pushrod-actuated springs, and separate lateral and heave dampers at both ends. Cadillac also gave it a race-inspired center screen that would give drivers with performance data and coaching as they learn the car. The connection to Cadillac's racing program is more than cosmetic. Since debuting in 2023, the V-Series.R has tallied 10 victories, 16 pole positions, and 32 podium finishes across IMSA and WEC competition. Its résumé includes the 2023 IMSA manufacturers', teams', and drivers' championships, the 2025 Le Mans Hyperpole, and Cadillac's first WEC 1-2 finish at São Paulo. Visually, the V-One remains remarkably close to the competition car, retaining much of its basic body and proportions. It does sport new V-Series wheels and darkened badging, as well as a hand-painted gradient that transitions from silver to deep navy. Inside, there is room for only one. The exposed carbon-fiber cockpit gets a custom-fitted driver's seat and a steering wheel whose button configuration can be tailored to the owner. Cadillac also incorporates more luxurious materials and a serialized plaque. Cadillac hasn't announced production plans, pricing, or how many V-Ones it might build. The company describes it as the "ultimate manifestation of a customer performance concept," which leaves the door conspicuously open.
