title: If Audi’s Nuvolari Isn’t Your Style, Spyker’s C8 Preliator Offers Audi V-8 Power with Classic Looks - Car and Driver
content: The latest supercar from the Dutch automaker packs a 789-hp twin-turbo V-8 borrowed from Audi and hooked up to a six-speed manual. Spyker has had a shaky existence. The original company, founded in 1880 as a carriage maker, transitioned to cars by 1900 but went out of business in 1926. Spyker was then revived in 1999 with a focus on ornate mid-engined supercars, but it has faced persistent financial issues, most recently filing for bankruptcy in 2021. But the Dutch automaker has returned once again, now unveiling its latest creation, the C8 Preliator XXV Coupé, at The Quail during Monterey Car Week. This is not the first time Spyker has used the C8 name. The C8 was the modern Spyker’s first production model, and entered its third generation in 2016 as the C8 Preliator. While Spyker claims that the new C8 Preliator XXV is “an entirely new automobile” that was “conceived from a clean sheet of paper,” the styling is suspiciously similar to the last Preliator. That’s no bad thing, however. The handmade aluminum body is curvaceous and adorned with gleaming rose gold accents. As always, Spyker draws inspiration from the world of aviation, such as with the taillights that emulate fighter-jet afterburners. Grilles on the front and rear ends wear an intricate mesh, NACA ducts are carved into the bodywork in the front bumper and rear fender, and a vent is set deep in the hood between the ovoid headlights, which include LEDs that spell out XXV. The biggest change stylistically versus the previous C8 Preliator is the new tail fin, which pokes up from the back of the roof scoop. The C8 has long borrowed V-8 engines from Audi, and the latest Preliator maintains that tradition, employing a twin-turbocharged 4.0-liter V-8 from Audi that produces 789 horsepower and 737 pound-feet of torque. That’s almost double what the original, naturally aspirated C8 produced back in 2000. This engine is mated to a six-speed manual transmission that directs power exclusively to the rear wheels. Spyker claims a zero-to-62-mph time of 2.9 seconds and a top speed of over 217 mph. The curb weight is listed at 3147 pounds, and the C8 Preliator rides on unequal-length control-arm suspension at all four corners. Its 15.0-inch front brake rotors are clamped by Brembo four-piston calipers, while four-piston units are paired with 14.0-inch rear discs. The C8 Preliator continues the old-school mentality inside, where the only digital display is a head-up unit, with no other screens present. The aluminum dashboard houses a bevy of analog gauges, buttons, and switches, and the rose gold accents continue inside, paired with acres of rich quilted brown leather called Tuscan Saddle. And of course, Spyker has retained the exposed gear linkage that has been present in the C8 from the beginning. Every exterior panel on the C8 Preliator is formed by hand, and Spyker says this approach means that building a car takes 800 hours. Spyker says it will only build 25 examples of the C8 Preliator XXV Coupé. There’s no word on price, but given the decadent design and hand-built approach, we have to imagine the latest C8 Preliator is not cheap. title: Cadillac Reveals V-Series.R-Based V-ONE Concept Prototype - dailysportscar.com
content: ShareFacebook, Twitter, Google Plus, Pinterest, Email Cadillac has revealed the V-ONE, a single-seat concept prototype based on the brand’s V-Series.R LMDh that currently competes in IMSA and the FIA WEC. Rooted in performance engineering with shared V-Series.R foundations, the V-ONE Concept, according to Cadillac, “explores how competition hardware can be translated into a driver-focused experience, while reinforcing Cadillac’s broader race-winning story across design, performance and technology.” “The Cadillac V-ONE Concept is the ultimate manifestation of a customer performance concept and is a clear sign of our ambition for the Cadillac V-Series brand in the future,” said Dominic Najafi, executive design director, Global Cadillac. The V-ONE is rooted in Cadillac’s LMDh racing programme and the V-Series.R race car. Co-developed by Cadillac Design, Cadillac Racing and chassis constructor Dallara, the concept is designed to deliver factory-level prototype performance and technology. At the heart of the V-ONE is a V8 hybrid powertrain that shares foundations with the race and title-winning Cadillac V-Series.R. It has more power than its racing counterpart, but a (lightly) simplified hybrid system which acts more as a boost to engine power and a unique aerodynamic package combining elements of different V-Series.R iterations. The concept also shares an identical chassis to the LMDh and deeper race-bred architecture in areas such as suspension, transmission and select electronics. Even with that race-derived foundation, the V-ONE is intended to be easier to operate while maintaining a similar level of performance. The aim is for its lap times to be within about 10% of the V-Series.R’s. The V-ONE’s exterior remains faithful to its race-honed sibling, while introducing refined details that make the concept feel more advanced, more technical and more tailored to Cadillac’s luxury identity. A hand-sprayed paint gradient from silver to deep navy “reflects the journey from day to night during an endurance race.” Inside, the single-seat V-ONE Concept transforms pure prototype hardware into a fully bespoke, race-bred cockpit, blending exposed carbon structure with an immersive, custom UX/UI and deeply personalized materials to create an elevated expression of Cadillac performance luxury. The steering wheel design lends to the racecar experience, complete with a button layout tailored for clients and developed by racing engineers. Other interior details include thoug material selection, including Cadillac Collection recycled fabrics, a serialized plaque on the door and a seat customized to the driver’s specifications. The Cadillac V-ONE Concept will be on display at The Quail, A Motorsports Gathering in Carmel, California on August 14, 2026. There is no word on whether or not this concept will form the basis for a wider customer programme in the future, similar to Ferrari’s 499P Modificata and the McLaren’s MCL-HY GTR projects. title: Arsenal v Manchester City in Community Shield and athletics gold – follow with us - The Guardian
content: Here’s how to follow along with our coverage – the finest writing and up-to-the-minute reports Long gone are the days of an August football big bang, with all the major men’s leagues starting at 3pm on the Saturday after the Charity Shield. But in the wake of Scotland, the Carabao Cup and the National League (not forgetting assorted European qualifiers and the Super Cup), the venerable Football League itself is back – and with it Matchday live. Emillia Hawkins will look at the fallout from Friday night’s Wolves v Blackburn Championship opener (a repeat of the 1960 FA Cup final for even older nostalgia fans) and all the buildup to the rest of the programme. A Bolton v Preston derby kicks off the day’s second-tier programme, alongside League One and League Two games, though the bulk of matches kick off at the sacred hour of three o’clock. Oh, and she will also have all the latest transfer news and gossip across the men’s and women’s games. Send your thoughts to matchday.live@theguardian.com Football, and lots of it. The pick of the Championship matches is perhaps Middlesbrough v Lincoln: a side who just missed a return to the promised land hosting one that got there. Imps fans have not seen fulfilment of the spring’s “Tottenham away, olé, olé” chant but, having not played at this level since 1961, they will hardly be complaining at facing a club who were in the Premier League in 2016-17, the season that City won promotion from the National League. Scott Murray will have news from the Riverside and all the other grounds, starting with the end of the lunchtime kick-offs, with Leicester’s second ever season in the third tier starting at playoff-winning Notts County among the early League One games. It’s the penultimate night at the Alexander Stadium in Birmingham and there will be high home hopes for the men’s 100m relay at 9.33pm, after Romell Glave and Jeremiah Azu completed a British one-two in the individual event. A quarter of an hour later, Amy Hunt, the women’s double sprint gold medallist, will be targeting relay glory. Other British hopefuls include Amber Anning in the women’s 400m at 8.10pm and Jake Wightman in the men’s 1500m at 9.07pm. While Sean Ingle reports from the second city, Luke McLaughlin will guide you through the evening as it happens. Emillia Hawkins will be back after her Saturday morning stint to pick through that day’s events and look forward to an afternoon of action that includes the traditional Wembley curtain raiser. To the surprise of some, the Community Shield is taking place in Cardiff – not because the FA forgot to book Wembley but, it seems, because four nights of concerts from the Weeknd were more lucrative. Email matchday.live@theguardian.com with your views on whether Arsenal v Manchester City in what is now a glorified friendly carries any real significance for the new season, and anything your spies can tell us about Watford v Southampton and Burnley v West Ham. The champions take on the FA Cup winners as usual, but at the Principality Stadium for the first time since 2006, when Liverpool beat Chelsea 2-1. Twelve months ago the Reds were also taking part but went down on penalties to Crystal Palace after a 2-2 Wembley draw in which they led twice and a shootout in which Mohamed Salah disappointed with the opening kick, a set of circumstances that did, in fact, prove a harbinger of what was to come (albeit for a side who were very much still coming to terms with the death of Diogo Jota). This year Arsenal and post-Pep Manchester City lock horns, with Rob Smyth on minute-by-minute duty, while Ben Fisher and Ed Aarons report from the Welsh capital. The Championship game of the weekend is deemed by Sky to be a claret-and-blue derby, and a first English league game for Burnley’s new manager, the Belgian Nicky Hayen, a much-travelled coach in his 12th role in 13 years. In the away dugout is Nuno Espírito Santo, who couldn’t quite keep West Ham up last season. After five years of Burnley yo-yoing between the top two divisions, Hayen will have his work cut out to engender much optimism in a support base that knows too much about false dawns, while the visitors are in turmoil over events in the boardroom as well as on the pitch. Tim de Lisle is on the blog, and Will Unwin reports from Lancashire. It’s the last night of action in Birmingham and it could be a triumphant one for Britain, with a rack of relays. First up is the mixed 4x100m at 8.35pm, another chance for Britain’s individual champions to add to their earlier golds. In the men’s 4x4oom at 9.48pm, Britain has the individual champion in Matt Hudson-Smith, while Amber Anning should be the star of the women’s quartet 15 minutes earlier. Individually, Georgia Hunter Bell is in the women’s 1500m at 9.13pm, while Sweden’s pole vault showman Mondo Duplantis is in action from 7.30pm. Sean Ingle is report from Birmingham agains while Billy Munday has the live blog.

title: Cadillac Says This V-One Concept Could Become a Real Car You Can Buy - MotorTrend
content: A personal car based on the V-Series.R Racer? Cadillac says it could happen. Among the tantalizing things Cadillac announced at this year’s Monterey Car Week is the V-One concept you see here. At first glance, the V-One looks a lot like the V-Series.R racing car that Cadillac fields at IMSA and FIA World Endurance Championship races. But the interior is quite the step up from your typical racing-car carbon tub, and the dynamics are meant to be accessible by mere mortals. Is the V-One a future production model? Cadillac was quick to emphasize that this is merely a concept for a track-focused vehicle. That said, it is not a hint at entry into a new racing series, nor something that will be offered for sale to a deep-pocketed racing team. So, is it a future customer car? Cadillac told us that “customer interest will inform future decisions.” Remember that the V-One debuted at the Quail, along with a gorgeous one-off Celestiq and on the heels of the announcement of the “Curated by Cadillac” personalization program. The Quail is where people who can afford specialized roadgoing racers tend to gather. And the people who run Cadillac are not dummies. It sounds like Cadillac could be making a serious come-on to the well-heeled. Power for the V-One concept comes from a V-8-based hybrid drivetrain that delivers 830 horsepower combined, with no finer details except that it “shares its foundations” with the V-Series.R (we assume “foundations” means the 5.5-liter DOHC V-8). Several suspension components are shared with the racing car, including the double-wishbone pushrod-actuated layout. The idea, Cadillac says, is to deliver the racing car’s performance without the driver requiring trained-racing-driver skill. At first glance, the interior might look racing-car spec, what with minimal switches and a steering wheel that looks as much like a smartphone as anything else. However, Cadillac describes the cockpit as—and we’re going to quote directly from the release because, frankly, the words make us salivate—“an intuitive, race-inspired interface and data visualization concept that gives drivers clear feedback and coaching as they explore the car’s full capability.” Did you get what we did from that? Rather than having the computers keep the driver out of trouble, the V-One will (er, could if it gets produced) coach the driver to learn to keep themselves out of trouble. Nice to know there are automakers who don’t necessarily assume self-driving cars are the only future. Cadillac also said that the button layout could be tailored to a client’s specification, as could the driver’s seat. Yes, Cadillac referred to potential buyers as “clients,” same as Ferrari and Rolls-Royce. Curated by Cadillac, indeed. Rich people of the world, you have your assignment: Go tell Cadillac that if it builds a machine like this, you’ll buy it. You will, won’t you? title: The Cadillac V-One Concept Previews What a Roadgoing Le Mans Race Car Could Look Like - Car and Driver
content: If you’d like to park an LMDh prototype car in your garage, the V-One concept shows the way. Last year, when Porsche debuted the 963 RSP—a street-friendlier version of its 963 hybrid race car built for Roger Penske—Cadillac evidently took notice. Because the V-One Concept, unveiled today at The Quail,  follows the same ideological path, which is essentially, “What if we made our race car a little bit more comfortable and people could maybe drive it on the dang road?” This is, of course, an excellent proposition and a thought experiment that we fully support, even if the chances of Cadillac selling Dallara-monocoque Le Mans racers at our local dealers are probably about the same as the likelihood of reviving the Cimarron. But feel free to place your Polymarket bets now. Cadillac hasn’t explicitly said that the V-One is intended for street use, but if that weren’t the case, then why not just offer the racer as a track toy and call it a day? Ferrari already does it with the 499P Modificata, after all. Cadillac says that, compared to its V-Series.R race car, the V-One is “intended to be easier to operate while offering a similar level of performance.” We think the V-One would be significantly quicker than its race brethren, given that it’s unconstrained by pesky LMDh class rules that limit the V-Series.R to 670 total horsepower. The V-One, meanwhile, is good for 830 combined horsepower from its 5.5-liter DOHC V-8 and electric motor, and while Caddy hasn’t specified which wick got turned up, we’d suspect it was on the loud side given that LMDh cars use a standardized 67-horsepower Bosch motor-generator unit. Carryover hardware from the race car consists of most of it, including the Dallara carbon-fiber monocoque, the body, and the pushrod-actuated suspension. And, like the V-Series.R, the V-One is a single-seater, but the interior has been poshed up a bit with Cadillac Collection fabrics, a custom user interface (read: screen), and steering wheel buttons that could be tailored to a customer’s desires—you know, if there were customers. The seat would, of course, be fitted to whoever is shelling out what the V-One would cost, which we estimate would be more than a CT4. Lest you confuse your V-One with all those V-Series.Rs strewn about the Target parking lot, the concept gets unique wheels, V badging, and a sweet paint job that transitions from silver at the front end to deep navy blue at the rear to symbolize day turning to night in an endurance race. Can we figure out how to offer that on Blackwings? There is also a serialized plaque on the door. Which implies more than one V-One, doesn’t it? We hope so. Because even if nobody figures out how to put a license plate on an LMDh car, it would make for an excellent way to spice up your next HPDE run group at your local road course. And if a production V-One seems unlikely, it wasn’t so long ago that the same could be said of Cadillac building our favorite 668-hp rear-drive sport sedans. Hey, dare to dream. title: Cadillac V-One Concept Previews A Rivalry Against The Wildest Ferraris And McLarens Customers Can Buy - CarBuzz
content: In the last 20 years, automakers have arguably found the limits of what can be done with a road car, and that's led many to shift to making special track-only supercars with hardly any limits on them. That presents a problem: how do you outdo a no-limits track car? The answer some automakers such as Porsche and McLaren have settled on is to turn actual race cars into something for the average rich buyer. Now, Cadillac may join them. Cadillac calls this car the V-One Concept, and it follows the rough formula set by Porsche's one-off 963 RSP for Roger Penske, and the McLaren MCL-HY GTR. It's effectively the LMDh race car that competes in IMSA WeatherTech SportsCar Championship in the US and Canada, and FIA World Endurance Championship overseas, but given the bare minimum of finishing to make it a bit less intimidating and rough for the buyer. It has the same Dallara chassis as the V-Series.R. It has the same pushrod-actuated double-wishbone suspension as the V-Series.R. It only has room for one driver, sits on center-lock wheels, and has the same body as, yes, the V-Series.R. Most importantly, it has the same powertrain, too, a naturally-aspirated 5.5-liter, double-overhead-cam V8 paired with an electric motor. In part because it's still a hybrid, it makes 830 horsepower, 110 more than the McLaren MCL-HY, which ditches the hybrid motor for the private customer vehicle. That's not to say there haven't been any changes. The exterior doesn't have quite as many lights nestled into the front end as the actual race cars. Cadillac also finished it with a gradient paint scheme that was done by hand, and it has unique wheels not shared with the race cars. The interior received the most attention, though. Race car interiors are entirely function over form, and Cadillac put a little effort into sanding down the rough edges. The dashboard has been given a little bit of aesthetic shaping, plus a strip of ambient lighting that's matched at the base of the center console. The single seat has also been spruced up and features upholstery from the Cadillac Collection, which is made from recycled materials. Still, the V-One's cabin is bare bones and remains similar to the race car with a steering yoke complete with telemetry display and controls, and the dash has big, basic buttons. You won't be confusing this for a Celestiq. Cadillac building just one of these V-Ones or even a short run for a few wealthy buyers could just be considered a special opportunity, rather than some indication of the future, since the company knows how to build them and can surely price them to cover the cost. However, Cadillac Executive Design Director Dominic Jajafi had an interesting statement about the concept. "The Cadillac V-ONE Concept is the ultimate manifestation of a customer performance concept and is a clear sign of our ambition for the Cadillac V-Series brand in the future." -Dominic Jajafi, Cadillac Executive Design Director That's a broad statement, and it could go in many directions. We do, though, think it means that we could see more seriously performance-focused models come from Cadillac, particularly inspired by the brand's motorsport programs. Not only does Cadillac participate in endurance racing with the V-Series.R, it just started its first season in Formula 1 this year. As the brand builds its racing reputation, it would only make sense to offer road cars that channel a bit of that mentality. Those cars would probably be more like the Blackwing sedans of late than most of the other V cars that offer some broad handling upgrades, but are mostly high-power GTs than actual sports cars. If you permit us to do a little wishful speculation, we could even see Cadillac creating a car based on the Corvette. It did so before with the XLR convertible, which was effectively a C5 Corvette with a retractable hardtop and a Northstar double-overhead-cam V8. In fact, a version of the Grand Sport X hybrid would be able to claim some similarities to the V-Series.R race car, being a mid-engine V8 hybrid. Just give it Cadillac styling and an extra-luxurious interior, and call it a day. Of course, we want to emphasize we're just daydreaming with this idea, and we'll just have to wait and see what Cadillac actually does. We want to hear from you. title: Cadillac's V-ONE Is a Le Mans Race Car You Can Commission - Top Speed
content: Cadillac pulled the wraps off the V-ONE Concept at The Quail, A Motorsports Gathering in Carmel, California on August 14 — a single-seat, hybrid hypercar study that doesn't just borrow the look of the brand's race cars but shares their actual bones. Built in collaboration with Cadillac Design, Cadillac Racing, and chassis constructor Dallara, the V-ONE is the first single-seat concept the brand has ever produced, and it makes a pointed statement: Cadillac's performance credentials come from the track, not the marketing department. At the center of the concept is an 830-horsepower hybrid V-8 that shares its foundational architecture with the V-Series.R LMDh race car — the same car that has collected 10 wins, 16 pole positions, and 32 podiums since its 2023 debut. That racing momentum includes the full sweep of the 2023 IMSA WeatherTech Championship manufacturer, team, and driver titles, plus the 2025 Le Mans Hyperpole and Cadillac's first 1–2 finish in the FIA World Endurance Championship at São Paulo. The V-ONE is, in effect, a distillation of all of it into a single driver's seat. The distinction Cadillac is drawing with the V-ONE is deliberate. The concept shares suspension components directly with the V-Series.R, including double wishbone geometry front and rear, pushrod-actuated coil and torsion spring elements, and lateral and heave dampers at both ends — the same setup that handles endurance stints at Le Mans and Sebring. Transmission architecture and select electronics also carry over from the race program. The aerodynamic package follows the V-Series.R's lead as well, with body proportions that Cadillac says carry directly from the race car to give the concept an authentic foundation rather than a stylized approximation. Even the driver interface reflects that philosophy: an intuitive, race-inspired UX and data visualization system is designed to give real-time feedback and coaching as a driver explores the car's full performance envelope. Cadillac says the V-ONE is intended to be easier to operate than the race car while maintaining a comparable level of performance. Inside, the single-seat cabin is where the concept's luxury credentials come into focus. The structure is exposed carbon fiber, and the steering wheel layout was developed by racing engineers specifically for client use — button placement and all. The seat is customized to each driver's individual specifications, and material choices include fabrics from the Cadillac Collection's recycled textile line. A serialized plaque on the door reinforces the one-of-one character the name promises. The UX and UI system is designed as an immersive layer over the race-derived hardware, translating prototype data into something a performance-focused owner can actually use on a circuit day. It's a cockpit that takes the V-Series.R's functional austerity and adds a level of personalization that makes it feel like a bespoke commission rather than a stripped race car. Externally, the V-ONE stays close to the V-Series.R's dramatic silhouette but introduces a handful of details that push it toward the luxury end of the spectrum. A new V-Series wheel design and updated dark-persona V-Series badging give the concept a more tailored character, while the most visually striking element is a hand-sprayed paint gradient that transitions from silver to deep navy — a reference, Cadillac says, to the journey from daylight to darkness over the course of an endurance race. "The Cadillac V-ONE Concept is the ultimate manifestation of a customer performance concept and is a clear sign of our ambition for the Cadillac V-Series brand in the future," said Dominic Najafi, Executive Design Director, Global Cadillac. The concept will remain on display at The Quail through August 14, with no production timeline announced — this is a concept study, not a production commitment, though the specificity of its engineering suggests Cadillac is testing appetite for exactly this kind of halo machine. title: Cadillac’s V-One Concept Refines the Brand’s Pole-Sitting Le Mans Racer - Road & Track
content: The more stately V-One softens up Cadillac’s Le Mans pole-sitter and IMSA champion, the V-Series.R. Whether at Le Mans, Daytona, and a dozen other race tracks across the world, Cadillac’s name is synonymous with an almighty roar. The V-Series.R, the current LMDh-spec racer that Cadillac factory programs run in IMSA GTP and the FIA World Endurance Championship, is a fan favorite in part because of the absurd noise it makes when its naturally-aspirated V-8 bump stops off all-electric power. As of Friday, Cadillac is imagining what that iconic powertrain would look like in a very different context. This is the V-One, the latest Monterey Car Week presentation from Cadillac. It is being called a concept, but Cadillac Executive Design Director Dominic Nafaji also calls it “a clear sign of our ambition for the Cadillac V-Series brand in the future.” Whether or not that means Cadillac actually plans to sell customers a refined version of its V-One, it feels like a good sign that the brand imagines more naturally-aspirated track cars going forward in one way or another. Aside from a unique two-tone finish of silver and dark blue, the exterior of the V-One should look extremely familiar to anyone who has seen the V-Series.R on track. The V-One even carries a low-mounted rear wing, a hallmark of the V-Series.R only since its aerodynamic platform was updated for the start of the 2026 IMSA season. Everything else, from the massive fin on the back of the engine cover to the flying buttress-like winglets attached only to the inside of all four fenders, carries over from the race car. Things turn more unique inside, where Cadillac has followed Porsche’s one-off 963 RSP by refining the sharp edges of the spartan cabin of what would otherwise be a race car. Softer materials, including recycled fabrics, cover some of the hard carbon fiber surfaces someone might expect to find on a race car. A steering wheel specific to the V-One sits at the center, running what Cadillac calls “an intuitive, race-inspired interface and data visualization concept.” In other words, the car’s user interface has also been adjusted to be more accommodating to potential private owners. Performance comes from that familiar 5.5-liter V-8 as part of a hybrid powertrain, producing a combined 830 horsepower in this application. Suspension components are shared with the race car, as well. To be sure, the V-One is not exactly a V-Series.R road car, even in concept form. Instead, this is best thought of as Cadillac’s slightly more plush answer to the Ferrari 499P Modificata or the Aston Martin Valkyrie LM—a variant of a Le Mans racer built with a customer in mind. Even that is still theoretical, though. This is just a concept for now, one debuting at The Quail, a Motorsports Gathering as part of Monterey Car Week. We’ll have to wait to see if Cadillac has anything more planned for this particular evolution of its race-winning prototype. See more photos of the Cadillac V-One Concept here. title: The Old Cadillac Is Dead, And This Track-Only V-One Concept Is The Proof - Jalopnik
content: The transformation of Cadillac is now complete. The GM luxury brand was once known for staid and vanilla chariots preferred almost exclusively by octogenarians in Boca Raton. For over 25 years the American automaker has been reinventing itself to not only compete with its German rivals, but best them in terms of speed, luxury, and design on the street and in competition at the race track. Not everything has gone swimmingly for Cadillac over the last two and a half decades, but it has certainly shucked its retiree image in favor of a more exciting heart-pounding future. The new V-One concept, essentially a customer-focused version of its race-winning prototype race car, is the final nail in the coffin of boring Caddy. Cadillac has been racing in IMSA's top class since 2017, and running the current Dallara chassis V-Series.R since the advent of the GTP ruleset in 2022. The V-Series.R has won ten races since it first set a wheel on track, competing against the best Acura, BMW, Porsche, Ferrari, Toyota, Lamborghini, Aston Martin, and others could throw at them. The new V-One concept takes a look at what it might be like for Cadillac to sell a handful of V-Series.R to well-heeled clients with a penchant for fast track days. "The Cadillac V-One Concept is the ultimate manifestation of a customer performance concept and is a clear sign of our ambition for the Cadillac V-Series brand in the future," said Dominic Najafi, Cadillac's executive design director. Cadillac worked hard to create a hard-edged prototype race car, but refined it for customers who don't necessarily have the on-track talent levels of Earl Bamber or Filipe Albuquerque. With a "race-derived foundation," Cadillac says the V-One is "easier to operate" than its V-Series.R race car, "while maintaining a similar level of performance." Like its V-Series.R siblings, the V-One is powered by a rowdy V8 engine with a hybrid system bumping the power significantly. The race car is limited by regulations to just 671 horsepower combined, with the spec Bosch MGU hybrid system delivering just 67 hp at peak. Without the need to fit into IMSA or the World Endurance Championship's rules, the V-One can pump up both the gas-powered V8 and the electric motor to gain an additional 159 ponies. Even if you don't know exactly how to extract the most from your car on track, this car will give you a chance at running within spitting distance of the pros, given the extra power. Cadillac doesn't say much about the engineering under the body, aside from the aero and suspension being "inspired by V-Series.R." That suspension is listed as a double-wishbone setup with pushrod-actuated coil and torsion spring elements with lateral and heave dampers on the front and rear. If you don't know what that means, just make sure you hire some mechanics to set the car up for you instead of just twisting knobs and hoping you got it right. Visually, the V-One is nearly identical to Cadillac's full-fat race car, carrying all of the aerodynamic enhancements, flicks, shark fins, and big wings. Instead of carrying sponsors and a race livery, however, the concept has a striking hand-sprayed paint job that gradients from silver at the front to deep navy blue at the rear, reflecting "the journey from day to night during an endurance race." There are also special wheel designs and V-Series badges on the exterior, making it look a little extra special. Cadillac also mentions a serialized plaque on the door, which hints at a small run of production cars. The highlight of this car, for me, is found in the interior. While similar to the race car's interior, Cadillac took the time to clean things up and remove a few of the adjustments the pros get. Cadillac's customers will be looking for a more refined driving experience than a pure race car. The seat will be customized to the driver's specification, the button layout on the steering wheel can be modified to fit the driver as well. And, of course, Cadillac will allow you to choose from a wide variety of materials to make your V-One as unique as possible. Don't worry about premium audio or infotainment, there won't be any. Cadillac is officially calling the V-One a concept car with no commitment to actually building these for customers. With it unveiling amongst the wealthy at The Quail during Monterey Car Week, it stands to reason, however, that Cadillac is testing the waters with potential clients who might be interested in dropping seven figures on a car like this one. If you've always wanted to be the fastest guy at your local SCCA track day, this is probably the car for you. This will probably be an extremely rare car produced in small handfuls. There probably aren't many people who could handle 830 horsepower, Michelin slicks, and high-downforce aero anyway. It's in the same vein as Porsche's one-off 963 RSP or Ferrari's $5.4-million 499P Modificata. It isn't a race car, and it certainly isn't a street car, so this car will have limited use for whoever would theoretically buy it. Unlike Ferrari, Cadillac doesn't currently have a Corse Clienti-style program to give customers an outlet to exercise these cars, but it certainly has the resources to whip one up. So far no word has been said as to whether this car will be available to order, or when, or what you can do with it once you do order one. There is also no mention of price, lap time, or who might even be eligible to order one once the books open up. Cadillac does have a long history of putting together concept cars that look basically ready for production without any kind of commitment to actually building them. I, for one, hope that Cadillac pushes this one out into the world, and whoever buys one actually takes it out for track exercise on the regular. This is the kind of car that deserves to be seen.

title: Cadillac’s V-One Hints At Track-Focused Hypercar That Won’t Step On The Corvette - Carscoops
content:
Cadillac's latest concept is essentially a consumer version of the V-Series.R race car Cadillac fans have been clamoring for a Corvette-based sports car for years, but they’ve apparently set their sights too low. That’s clear today as the company is hinting at a hypercar inspired by their V-Series.R race car. Looking fresh off the track, the V-One is the “ultimate manifestation of a customer performance concept and is a clear sign of our ambition for the Cadillac V-Series brand in the future.” More: Cadillac Just Built Its Most Powerful Blackwing Ever While most high-performance models simply borrow cues from race cars, the concept was jointly created by Cadillac Design, Cadillac Racing, and Dallara. This means it has racecar DNA in its blood and shares its “foundations” with the model that competes in the FIA World Endurance Championship as well as the IMSA WeatherTech Championship. Power comes from a hybridized V8 powertrain that echoes the V-Series.R. Cadillac didn’t say much about it, but it presumably consists of a naturally aspirated 5.5-liter V8, a 1.35 kWh battery pack, a seven-speed sequential transmission, and an electric motor. Specifics are hazy, but the company confirmed a combined output of 830 hp (619 kW / 842 PS). That’s actually more than the race car, which is limited to 670 hp (500 kW / 679 PS). The similarities to the V-Series.R don’t stop there, as a number of components are shared with the race car. This includes the double wishbone suspension as well as “pushrod-actuated coil and torsion spring elements with lateral and heave dampers.” While the model borrows heavily from the race car, your typical tech bro doesn’t have the same skill set as driver Jack Aitken. As a result, the V-One is “intended to be easier to operate,” while still maintaining a similar level of performance to the V-Series.R. On the styling front, the body carries over from the racer to give the concept an “authentic foundation.” It looks wild and features a custom paint job, which smoothly transitions from silver to deep navy. Elsewhere, there are unique wheels that are wrapped in Michelin Pilot Sport tires and backed up by a high-performance Brembo braking system. The model also features “dark-persona” V-Series badging as well as plenty of carbon fiber. The interior has a clear link to motorsports, but the cabin is more welcoming and luxurious. There’s a single seat, which uses recycled fabrics and can be customized to fit the driver. To their right is an exposed carbon fiber shelf, which can hold a helmet. While race cars typically have a bewildering number of controls, Cadillac seems to have found a nice middle ground. Drivers sit behind a yoke-style steering wheel with an integrated display. The latter is flanked by shifter lights, dials for the hybrid system and brakes, as well as a number of buttons. Cadillac didn’t say much about the interior, but the steering wheel display has an “intuitive, race-inspired interface.” It also “gives drivers clear feedback and coaching as they explore the car’s full capability.” While the V-One is clearly a concept, it’s exciting to see Cadillac exploring the possibility of a track-focused hypercar. title: BTS’ V Opens Up About Hearing Loss - Kiss 95.1 Charlotte
content:
BTS’ V is used to hearing thousands of fans cheer his name. Now, the singer is opening up about a quieter and much more personal issue. The BTS member, whose… BTS’ V is used to hearing thousands of fans cheer his name. Now, the singer is opening up about a quieter and much more personal issue. The BTS member, whose real name is Kim Taehyung, revealed during a livestream on Wednesday, Aug. 12, that he has been experiencing hearing loss in one ear. He said he is receiving treatment and regularly visiting a doctor, according to The Korean Times, The Korean Herald and BBC. V gave fans a simple way to understand what he has been experiencing. “If my hearing on this ear is 100, the other ear can only pick up around 30,” V said, per the Korean Herald, while pointing to each ear in turn. “I’m regularly taking prescribed medicine and visiting the doctor often.” For someone whose career depends heavily on music, performing and connecting with crowds, the news is especially personal. Still, V did not present the update as a reason for fans to panic. Instead, he explained that he is taking his health seriously and getting medical care. V said this was the first time he had publicly told fans about his hearing loss, even though he has been dealing with it for “about two and a half” years. He said he first noticed his hearing getting worse while serving in the South Korean military. V served from Dec. 11, 2023, to June 10, 2025, per The Korean Herald. “This actually started while I was in the military, and after it got a bit worse,” he said. “Since I was surrounded by people who exercised a lot, everyone said, ‘It’s a matter of mental strength.’ “ V explained that he is now taking a different approach by putting his health first. Rather than simply trying to push through the problem, he said he is staying in contact with doctors and having his hearing checked. The singer said he was “going to the hospital regularly” to get his hearing checked, per The Korean Times. Hearing loss can happen for several different reasons, and it does not always look the same from one person to another. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) noted that there are four types of hearing loss, including conductive hearing loss. This type happens when something prevents sound from moving through the outer or middle ear. Depending on the cause, it can sometimes be treated with medicine. Another type is sensorineural hearing loss, which involves a problem with the inner ear or hearing nerve. Mixed hearing loss includes both conductive and sensorineural hearing loss. The CDC also says hearing loss can have many causes, including repeated exposure to loud sounds. According to Mayo Clinic, other possible causes include damage to the inner ear, a ruptured eardrum, an ear infection or unusual bone growths. Because V has not revealed the cause of his hearing loss, it would be impossible to say what specifically led to his condition. For now, the important part of his update is that he is getting treatment and keeping up with his doctors. Even with the health issue, V remains busy. He is currently touring with BTS as part of the group’s global Arirang Tour, which kicked off in Goyang, South Korea, in April. The group is currently touring North America, with upcoming dates in Chicago, Los Angeles and Toronto. BTS is scheduled to wrap up the Arirang Tour in the Philippines in March. For V, the road ahead includes plenty of stages, travel and music. But his latest update shows that he is also making room for something just as important: taking care of himself. After keeping his hearing struggles private for years, V decided to let fans in on what he has been dealing with. And while the news may have surprised many people, his message was fairly straightforward. He knows something is wrong, he is getting help, and he is not ignoring it. title: Live Oak Acquisition Corp. V Q2 Earnings Call Highlights - MarketBeat
content:
Live Oak Acquisition Corp. V NASDAQ: TMS, which operates as Teamshares, said it reaffirmed its 2026 outlook and expects acquisitions to be the primary contributor to growth after completing its Nasdaq listing in June. During its first earnings call as a public company, Teamshares reported that second-quarter revenue increased 20% year over year, primarily driven by acquisitions. The company’s last-12-month pro forma revenue reached $560 million, while SME segment EBITDA rose 47% from the prior-year period to $20 million. Co-founder and CEO Michael Brown said Teamshares, founded in 2019, is focused on acquiring small- and mid-sized businesses from retiring owners and holding them permanently. The company had grown to 93 companies and approximately $500 million in consolidated revenue as of the call. Teamshares reaffirmed its 2026 target of $40 million in acquired EBITDA and its $60 million pro forma adjusted EBITDA target. Brown described pro forma adjusted EBITDA as a run-rate measure assuming the company had owned all acquired businesses for the trailing 12-month period. As of Aug. 14, the company had 10 signed, mutually non-binding letters of intent representing approximately $30 million of new SME segment EBITDA. Alex Eu, co-founder and president, said the company’s typical closing process takes 90 to 120 days, and the businesses in the backlog average roughly $3 million of SME segment EBITDA. Teamshares acquired two businesses during the first half of 2026, representing about $2.6 million in SME segment EBITDA. Eu said acquisition activity was relatively light during the first half because the company was focused on completing its public listing and had constrained access to reasonably priced acquisition capital. CFO Brian Gaebe said the company expects about $30 million of the path to its $60 million pro forma adjusted EBITDA target to come from businesses currently under letters of intent. It is targeting at least another $9 million from businesses under evaluation but not yet under LOI, alongside modest organic growth and controlled corporate overhead. Management said acquisition closings in the small-business market tend to be weighted toward the second half of the year, particularly the fourth quarter. Brown said businesses often come to market after corporate taxes are filed in the spring, creating a natural timeline that pushes transaction closings later in the year. Eu said Teamshares evaluates its model through four core factors: deploying capital into durable businesses at attractive terms, preserving and growing acquired earnings, scaling corporate infrastructure more slowly than segment earnings, and improving financing access and cost of capital as the company grows. Organic revenue grew 3.4% in the second quarter and 4.2% year to date. Organic SME segment EBITDA grew 0.4% in the quarter and 4.6% year to date. Eu said management views year-to-date performance as more informative than quarterly results because of seasonality across its businesses. The company continues to use an annual organic growth framework of roughly 3% after the initial year of acquisition, according to management. Eu said Teamshares does not require synergies or aggressive growth for acquisitions to be attractive, as its underwriting generally assumes flat performance in the first year and modest growth afterward. Corporate costs declined by approximately $500,000 in the second quarter while SME segment EBITDA increased by $6.4 million, or 47%, according to Eu. He said the results demonstrate operating leverage from the company’s transaction, reporting, operating oversight and data infrastructure. Teamshares expects corporate overhead to increase by about $2 million in the second half of 2026, or roughly 10% compared with the second half of 2025, primarily due to public-company compliance costs, Gaebe said. Management emphasized that financing capacity remains the principal constraint on the company’s acquisition pace. Brown said Teamshares has sufficient sourcing activity and processing capacity, but that financing and cash flow are the main drivers and limiters of growth. Gaebe said Teamshares signed a term sheet in early August for a warehouse facility intended to provide committed capital for acquisition closings, including a material amount for companies already under LOI. The company is also evaluating alternatives to refinance existing debt and add capacity for longer-term growth. According to Gaebe, Teamshares has received multiple non-binding term sheets from potential lenders. Management did not disclose pricing or detailed terms for the financing proposals, citing their non-binding status. Brown said the company has seen increased interest from larger businesses within its target range, particularly those generating $2 million to $5 million in EBITDA. Teamshares historically focused on businesses with EBITDA between $500,000 and $5 million. On purchase valuations, Brown said current acquisition multiples remain generally consistent with last year. He noted that businesses in the $2 million to $5 million EBITDA range may trade closer to five to six times EBITDA, compared with a four-to-five-times range in other cases. The company reported an average acquisition multiple of 5.3 times in 2025. Eu said the company’s first quarter has historically been its weakest because of consumer spending patterns and winter weather affecting outdoor activities. First-quarter segment EBITDA has historically represented about 10% to 15% of annual EBITDA, while the second and third quarters have been the strongest. The fourth quarter has historically been below the second and third quarters but substantially above the first quarter. During the second quarter, Teamshares shut down one subsidiary that Eu described as subscale and not meaningful to results, with a purchase price below $1 million. He said the company has moved through a backlog of businesses that no longer met its evolving acquisition criteria and expects such exits to be more limited going forward. Brown said Teamshares’ priorities through year-end include completing capital transactions and debt refinancing, closing its targeted $40 million of acquired EBITDA while maintaining underwriting standards, advancing organic EBITDA growth, and continuing to build systems designed to create operating leverage. title: Kian v. Florida : The Right to Be Tried Before a Twelve-Person Jury - Cato Institute
content: Sign up to have blog posts delivered straight to your inbox! When Hamed Kian was charged in Florida with five counts of practicing chiropractic medicine with a suspended license—a felony carrying up to five years in prison—he was tried before a six-person jury. Convicted on all counts by this truncated panel, Mr. Kian appealed, arguing that Florida’s six-person jury rule deprived him of his right to a trial by a twelve-person jury as required by the Sixth and Fourteenth Amendments. The Florida appellate court affirmed his conviction without a written opinion, and Mr. Kian asked the US Supreme Court to review his case. In trying felony cases before six-person juries, Florida’s reliance on the Supreme Court’s 1970 decision in Williams v. Florida breaks from centuries of tradition. The Framers incorporated the common-law criminal jury into Article III and the Sixth Amendment as a vital structural check against government overreach, overzealous prosecution, and judicial bias. While the Constitution’s text does not explicitly specify a numerical requirement, the Court’s recent originalist jurisprudence—most notably in Ramos v. Louisiana—reaffirms that the Sixth Amendment protects the fundamental attributes the criminal jury possessed at common law. Historically, the requirement that a criminal petit jury consist of precisely twelve members remained undisputed in English and American law for hundreds of years until Williams improperly abandoned that historical scope. The Supreme Court granted Mr. Kian’s petition, and the Cato Institute filed an amicus brief in support of Mr. Kian. In our brief, we ask the justices to overrule Williams v. Florida and reverse the decision. Our brief stresses that the structural guarantees of the Bill of Rights cannot be subjected to arbitrary judicial interest-balancing or functionalist reduction. Restoring the common law twelve-person jury requirement is essential to protecting defendants’ constitutional rights, maintaining public confidence in judicial outcomes, and upholding the original meaning of the Sixth Amendment. title: A Conversation with Poetic V - Poetry Center
content:
Some voices don’t just write poetry; they carry it, live it, and use it to heal others in the process. Vanessa Williams, known as “Poetic V,” is a California-raised, Las Vegas-based poet, teacher, spoken word artist, and author whose work is rooted in truth, faith, and transformation. With more than ten poetry slam wins, performances across eight states, and stages including TEDx, South by Southwest, and the Las Vegas Book Festival, she has built a powerful presence that extends far beyond the mic. Through her writing and her book Poetically Affirmed, she uses her own life experiences to give voice to the voiceless and remind others that even grief has purpose, and healing is always within reach. Can you share a bit about your journey as a poet—what drew you to poetry and how your craft has evolved? My poetry journey began at the age of 10 in my 5th-grade writing class. The assignment was to write a poem about “Home.” Before this moment, I had never written a poem, so I was a bit nervous. An A+ and framed poem hanging in my room like an award later, something in me “clicked.” I found myself writing all the time. Short stories, poems, free writes, etc. In a home where emotions and feelings were prisoners, I found freedom in pen and paper. A year later, I joined a Performing Arts Ministry Group called Tribe of Judah World Outreach, where we traveled all over the world telling people about God through dance, step routines, and POETRY! I was able to encourage and help others through my experiences. In 2017, my mother passed away, and poetry shifted again. Tears filled pages more than words did, and I was reminded of how much I need to write. Understanding how important it is to release what is inside in order to really heal. In 2018, I moved to Las Vegas from Southern California, where I was introduced to poetry again. Not just for therapy or helping others, but also as a career. I get paid for this now! Lol. But in all seriousness, there's nothing like getting paid for something you love to do. In April 2021, I wrote and published my first book, “Poetically Affirmed”: A collection of ‘I Am’ poems to affirm you daily. I was dealing with so many emotions and I knew I wanted to be better than I was, so I wrote myself into the place I wanted to be. My poetry continues to evolve as I do, and sometimes before me. As if I am catching up to the poems. What poets make up your "literary family tree"? In other words, which poets or poems have been most meaningful to you as a writer of poetry? My literary family tree includes poets like Patricia Smith, Ebony Stewart, Rudy Francisco, Maya Angelou, and Ariana Brown. What draws me to each of them is their ability to tell the truth with both vulnerability and strength—to write in a way that moves people long after the poem ends. What does your writing process look like? Are there inspirations or experiences that guide your poetry? My writing process happens in two ways. One, getting a lightning stick of inspiration from something I've heard or seen, and I have to immediately write it out. Or two, having a topic I am passionate about and making time to write. I have fallen in love with editing. For a long time, I would never edit my poems. However they came out, that's what it was. Wild! I know. But now, I see how a poem really comes alive as it's dissected. Most of my writing comes from life experiences. Not to sound corny, but my life is my inspiration. From faith to love to women's rights, injustice among the black community, etc. It all comes from my heart to the ears and eyes of whoever is willing to listen and read. I know if I am facing something, someone else is as well, so let me write to uplift us both. Which of your works do you feel most deeply represents your voice, and what themes or messages are central to your poetry? I have a poem entitled “Eulogy for the Living.” It is so easy to only focus on what we have lost, who has left us, and where the holes are. But I realized in doing this, we miss who and what are still standing next to us. This poem is a thank you to my father and represents the raw emotions of grief, while not making it an idol where nothing else matters. Going through this, my faith was and still is being tested. I realized how little grief is talked about in Church. Or when it is talked about, it's met with a “just pray on it, you'll be alright.” But what happens when sorrow sucks the life out of you, and you can’t pray? I wasn't alright, and I wasn’t going to pretend. I began to write the truth about grief and faith. Telling the truth and giving hope. This has become the main focus of my poetry and ties in so many other topics such as identity, value, world views, etc. Are there recurring symbols, metaphors, or motifs that continue to appear across your body of work? What draws you back to them? I often use ocean or water metaphors. When it comes to the ocean, I love its duality. Calm yet can cause chaos. Can birth and destroy life. It is my favorite place on earth. My mom used to call me a ‘fish’ because once I was in that water, I wasn't coming out. We had that in common. Once she passed, her ashes were spread in the ocean, so now it's the place I feel most close to her. Water reminds me of the Holy Spirit, and many times in spiritual texts, his characteristics are those of water. How intentionally do you build visual landscapes within your poetry? For a long time, I just wrote. Whatever I felt, that was it. Didn’t even edit most of the time. I know; blasphemy. But now I want people to see the poem, not just hear it, and visuals make emotions tangible. If I’m talking about heartbreak, I don’t just want the audience to understand pain — I want them to feel like they’re standing inside the room where it happened. Imagery for me is one of the biggest parts of my writing process now. I think in scenes first. It’s like a movie. I often ask myself, “What does this emotion look like, sound like, smell like?” before I write. Whether it’s comparing grief to a cracked bone healing wrong or faith to being held underwater and still breathing, I use visual language to make abstract emotions easier to connect to. How do music, culture, memory, or personal history influence the texture and tone of your poetry? Music, culture, memory, and personal history shape every poem I write. I grew up understanding that stories carry power, and poetry became the place where my experiences, my faith, and my community could all meet. The rhythm of spoken word, gospel, and everyday conversations all find their way into my work. I don’t write just to tell my story—I write so someone else can find themselves in it. My poetry is rooted in healing, restoration, and purpose. Every piece is an opportunity to turn memory into meaning and remind people that even the hardest chapters can become part of a greater testimony. Is there a particular poem in your collection that challenged you technically or emotionally? What made it difficult to complete? I am currently writing a poem called “Who Told You God was White?” I’m very passionate about using my poetry to lead people to God, or at least curious enough to listen to the whole poem. This piece is so important to me because the narrative in most people's minds is that Christianity is a white man’s religion used as a weapon for manipulation and control. But that’s just not the truth. My desire with this piece is to provide factual information and evidence, while expressing God's heart for all. I want to be sensitive yet bold, truthful yet tactful. I’m excited and nervous. As a Black woman poet, how have you navigated visibility and recognition in the literary world? Have there been specific challenges or breakthroughs? Living in a city like Las Vegas, visibility and recognition as a black poet have actually been attainable. I truly believe this is because of so many black poets before me and the work they have done. When it comes to academia and publishing outside of Vegas, however, the hurdles are there. In 2024, only 5-6% of authors are black, and even a smaller number of those writers are poets. This is why articles like this are so important. We must be encouraged to write, submit, and publish despite rejection. And this has been my stance for years. The world will see and hear us whether they like it or not. How do you see your work contributing to broader conversations about Black identity, womanhood, or contemporary culture? My work contributes to these conversations because it unveils another side of the stories already being told. Like another patch in a quilt of black importance, my work brings comfort, warmth, and value to all who experience it, especially when it comes to black women and grief. There is such a notion that the black woman must always remain strong, in control, never tired or weary. But the truth is “Black Women Grieve.” My work gives a voice to those who are too busy or ashamed to speak. How has building relationships within literary communities or collaborating with other artists shaped your work and career? I owe 90% of my career to connecting with communities and collaborating with other artists. Before coming to Vegas, I never knew any of this was possible. Now the possibilities are endless. So many of the features, shows, and opportunities I have been awarded come from a connection or someone mentioning my name when I wasn't in the room. The way we are able to come together, learn from one another, and expand the reach of poetry is a poem all by itself. I have learned the power of connection and truly believe we were never meant to do this on our own. What makes a powerful slam poem? What makes slam different from poetry on the page? When I think of Slam poetry, I think of written poetry coming alive. It is no longer words echoed in your own voice as you read, but it has hands, feet, and a heartbeat you cannot ignore. Slam poetry gives the written words, without sounding cliché, a voice. It allows the poet to explore different tones and expressions of a poem. Experimenting with character and even adding theatrical elements. To me, slam poetry takes the limits off the artist. What guidance would you give to emerging Black women poets who are trying to find their voice, gain visibility, and make an impact in today’s literary landscape? First thing you must know beyond any doubt that would try to speak to you, whether inward or outward, your story is needed! There are hundreds of black women poets, but God only created one you. Secondly, gaining inspiration from other poets is vital and powerful, but do not think you must sound or write like others to be accepted or seen. The world needs your authenticity. Thirdly, become a master at this craft. Never stop learning, growing, and perfecting. And lastly, have fun! Remember why you write. Enjoy the journey and know somebody is being changed by your vulnerability! Vanessa Williams AKA “Poetic V” is a California raised, Las Vegas living Poet, teacher, spoken word artist and author. She has won over 10 poetry slams and has written and published her own poetry book Poetically Affirmed. Poetic V has had the privilege of being a featured artist in over 8 states and 30+ events, including the Las Vegas Book Festival, Miss Nevada African Pageant, 3x Utah Arts Festival performer, South by South West performer and a Tedx presenter. title: Understanding the court’s next major case on asylum seekers: Wassily v. Blanche - SCOTUSblog
content: This coming term, in Wassily v. Blanche, the Supreme Court will decide whether asylum beneficiaries are barred from obtaining lawful permanent residency if their asylum status has been terminated. Wassily is of considerable significance. While the termination of asylum status once was relatively uncommon, recent policy changes by the Trump administration have exposed far more immigrants to the risk of this. The legal dispute in Wassily, which has divided the federal courts, dates back to unclear language in the Refugee Act of 1980. The Refugee Act laid the framework for the modern asylum system and defined legal standards for asylum officers, immigration judges, and other immigration adjudicators. The act used precise, detailed language in crafting the refugee process for noncitizens outside of the United States, but Congress left internal asylum procedures more undefined, with less statutory guidance. Over time, asylum claims increased dramatically, making unclear statutory gaps more and more troublesome. Indeed, that lack of statutory clarity is front and center in Wassily. The Refugee Act specified that refugees processed outside the United States could only obtain a permanent resident green card if their refugee “admission has not been terminated.” By contrast, the act was unclear whether that same requirement also applied to asylees who had obtained asylum status from within the United States. For asylees applying to “adjust” to permanent resident status, as codified at 8 U.S.C. § 1159(b), the Refugee Act did not mention termination at all. Instead, the act only said that the immigration official “may” grant the green card for “any alien granted asylum” who met the admissibility requirements. The act did not say whether “granted asylum” meant anyone who previously had been granted asylum or whether that phrase was limited to those with a current asylum status. Tamer Wassily left his native Egypt and entered the United States in 1993. He was granted asylum in 2000 based on his claim of persecution in Egypt as a Coptic Christian. Later, he was convicted of stalking and child endangerment, at which point the DHS sought to terminate his asylum status before an immigration judge. The immigration judge agreed and terminated this based on the finding that Wassily’s stalking conviction was a “particularly serious crime.” But the immigration judge found him eligible to adjust to a green card because the immigration statute did not contain “an explicit requirement” of current asylum status. Byron Velasquez Arreaga entered the United States in 1995 and was granted asylum. He later was convicted of multiple crimes for driving while intoxicated. The DHS sought to terminate his asylum status and scheduled an immigration court hearing. The immigration judge terminated his asylum status for particularly serious crimes. In contrast to Wassily’s immigration judge, this immigration judge found that without a current asylum status, Velasquez Arreaga could not adjust status to a green card and he was ordered removed to his native country of Guatemala. The parties appealed both cases. The Board of Immigration Appeals weighed in on the statutory confusion in a precedent decision: Matter of T-C-A-. The BIA interpreted the statute as meaning that only a noncitizen with current asylum status could adjust to permanent resident status. In Wassily’s appeal, the BIA relied on Matter of T-C-A-. It found that Wassily’s terminated asylum status made him ineligible for adjustment to a green card. The BIA also found Velasquez Arreaga ineligible for adjustment. In tandem cases for Wassily and Velasquez Arreaga, a divided panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit agreed with the majority of circuits that only noncitizens with current asylum status were eligible for asylee adjustment. The 2nd Circuit concluded that the statutory phrase “granted asylum” was best understood to require a current asylum “status” – a legally significant term as used by Congress. The panel majority said its reading was “buttressed” by statutory context, including the Immigration Act of 1990. That act explicitly created a time-restricted exception that allowed some noncitizens to apply for green cards “regardless of whether or not such asylum has been terminated.” The circuit reasoned that this limited exception, as a “statutory note,” did not create a general rule that noncitizens could apply for permanent residency after termination. In dissent, Judge Beth Robinson adopted the minority view of the circuits on this “difficult” statutory question. She reasoned that the asylee adjustment statute meant that “any” noncitizen was eligible to adjust who previously had been granted asylum. Under Robinson’s view, the absence of the word “status” from the statutory provision must have been an intentional omission by Congress. The Supreme Court granted certiorari in June to review the statutory question of whether terminated asylees are eligible to apply for adjustment to permanent residency. In their petition for certiorari, Wassily and Velasquez Arreaga argue that the statutory text and context are clear that any noncitizen who was “granted asylum” previously can seek permanent residence after termination. They interpret “granted” as a past tense verb, and they contend that the omission of “status” in the statutory language must be given effect because Congress knew how to include such a requirement. As broader statutory context, Wassily and Velasquez Arreaga emphasize the adjacent Section 1159(c), which allows for a discretionary “waiver” of other requirements for the noncitizen’s admissibility. According to them, it would be “strange” to interpret the statute as “categorically” stripping the attorney general of that discretionary authority where the asylee’s status has been terminated. Wassily and Velasquez Arreaga also invoke the rule of lenity – the canon that a statutory ambiguity should be construed in favor of the noncitizen. They claim that lenity is especially paramount after the Supreme Court’s 2024 decision in Loper Bright v. Raimondo, which eliminated the doctrine of Chevron deference to a federal agency’s (here, the BIA’s) reasonable interpretation of an ambiguous statute. In an atypical move where only the U.S. Courts of Appeals for the 2nd, 4th, and 5th Circuits so far have looked at this issue, Solicitor General D. John Sauer agrees that the Supreme Court should grant review. Even so, the solicitor general maintains that the 2nd Circuit was correct in interpreting asylee adjustment as limited to noncitizens with current asylum status. The government says that Congress’ intent is best understood as giving effect to the termination of asylum “status” as a bar to obtaining a green card. The solicitor general relies on the statutory note in the Immigration Act of 1990 as evidence that Congress only excepted a small subset of asylees from the general rule barring terminated asylees from adjustment of status. Without citing Loper Bright, the government disputes that the rule of lenity is applicable here at all. The solicitor general argues that the discretionary waiver at Section 1159(c) does not undermine the most natural reading of asylee adjustment because “the decision to terminate is itself discretionary” and the court should give effect to that waiver authority. The Supreme Court’s resolution of this case could impact the interests of the millions of asylum applicants with cases pending in the immigration courts and asylum offices, as well as those persons granted asylum status in recent years. Even if the Supreme Court narrowly frames this case as a discrete statutory question, it will clarify the effect of the government’s termination authority for anyone granted asylum. This is especially timely: in December 2025, the DHS announced that it would “comprehensively re-review” asylum approvals from “high-risk” countries since entry in 2021. At the end of that review, the DHS could elect to terminate asylum status. In June 2026, a federal district court vacated the DHS re-review policy, but the government is challenging that ruling. That’s not all. The case also could have broader implications for federal administrative law if the justices take an interest in the parties’ arguments about the government’s discretionary authority or Loper Bright. The Supreme Court has not yet relied on Loper Bright in deciding an immigration case. In fairness, the 2nd Circuit found no need to do so, and the Supreme Court avoided a similar issue in Urias-Orellana v. Bondi, a case that concerned the judicial standard of review for asylum “persecution” determinations. But that does not mean the court will continue to let this issue linger. Disclosure: When he was at the DOJ, the author litigated Wassily before the 2nd Circuit. He no longer has any involvement in the case or its litigation before the Supreme Court. Duncan Fulton is an Assistant Professor at Loyola University New Orleans College of Law. He has litigated more than 100 immigration cases in federal courts nationwide. title: The McLaren McL 6GT Concept Previews a Stick-Shift V-8 Hypercar for 2028 - MotorTrend
content: A manual gearbox immediately separates McLaren’s latest hypercar from most of its potential rivals. It’s difficult for automakers to stand out during the annual Car Week in Monterey, California, where you can’t throw an Amex black card without hitting yet another new supercar or hypercar. McLaren managed the feat with the unveiling of its new McL 6GT, a clean-lined concept car with an honest-to-goodness manual transmission. But it’s not just a concept, as the Car Week version presages a production model scheduled to arrive in 2028. Its buyers will be able to snap through the gears just like in the fabled F1, the hypercar whose 1996 GTR version is expected to fetch roughly $35 million during Saturday’s RM Sotheby’s Monterey Auction. The cranberry-red McL 6GT concept seems focus-grouped for Car Week itself, and not just for the wealthy enthusiasts and collectors that haunt the peninsula’s manicured lawns. The manual come-on—a stick tease?—will have car lovers of all ages and incomes Googling the last modern supercars with a clutch pedal aboard. And the McLaren’s six-speed manual transmission seems as good of a way as any for the marque to create separation from a herd of rivals. According to the company, the McL 6GT blends “purity of character with lightweight carbon-fiber construction, V-8 internal combustion power, and for the first time in a McLaren since the legendary F1, an authentic manual transmission sending drive to the rear wheels.” After years of post-Covid financial and sales struggles, McLaren Automotive was acquired in April 2025 by Abu Dhabi’s CYVN Holdings and integrated with the luxury EV startup Forseven.  For the past 16 months, executives said, McLaren has mostly stayed quiet, reflecting on its strategies for producing vehicles and better serving its customers. Now that quiet period is ending, with the McL 6GT the first stop on a roadmap of new models. The company seems intent on playing up a history that may not be as familiar as that of, say, Enzo Ferrari’s. Nick Collins, chief executive officer, invoked its eponymous, New Zealand-born founder as being a similar guiding light for making decisions. “We are literally just getting started, and with the maverick spirit of Bruce [McLaren],” Collins said. The McL 6GT name may read like a vanity plate. But with two extra letters, it reinterprets another seminal McLaren. Indeed, the M6GT that shared the car’s reveal stage was Bruce McLaren’s personal car in the late 1960s, and his ambitious vision for turning his M6A Can-Am racer into a roadgoing car. But McLaren was killed in 1970 at age 32 while testing the McLaren M8D Can-Am car at the Goodwood Circuit. The M6GT project died with him, and it would be another 22 years before McLaren made the transition to the street with the F1. McLaren executives say the new car realizes its founder’s unfulfilled dream, but with six subsequent decades of innovation woven in—including a woven carbon-fiber monocoque that underpins every modern McLaren. “In every case, we asked ourselves, ‘What would Bruce have done?’” said Kemal Curic, the brand’s new chief design officer. The concept aims to meld the race-inspired styling of 1960s sports prototypes with modern execution and packaging. A low, wide footprint evokes the stance of the M6GT’s own progenitor, the M6A Can-Am racer. Clean, uninterrupted body surfaces flow from the low snout to a Kamm back tail. The right-hand-drive concept flashed a carbon-fiber body with smoothly integrated aerodynamic functions. An unadorned lower front inlet sends air rushing through a cavernous hood duct and over a slim greenhouse. Rear glass incorporates vents and exposed fasteners. LED-ringed front inlets and air curtains help with cooling. Low-set, finned side intakes feed a mid-mounted V-8 whose displacement and specs remain a company secret for now. Elongated, subtly swelling rear fenders flow into an appealingly integrated rear spoiler. An upswept carbon-fiber splitter armors the rear below striking convex taillamps in a motif Curic calls a “continuous racetrack.” It’s a kind of tightly squeezed oval that’s repeated on exhaust outlets, front intakes, interior vents, and even seatbelt fasteners. Oversized headlamp lenses pay homage to the Can-Am-based original. Dihedral doors pivot over complex side sills in exposed carbon fiber. The flowing body sits atop star-shaped wheels and Pirelli P Zero R tires, including 325/30/R21s at the rear. Inside, “boxed quilting” with seat upholstery in a stitched grid pattern, gets a modern glow-up in Alcantara. The thick synthetic suede blankets a portion of the door sills, a fine padded perch for your butt as you swing your legs inside. The McL 6GT is designed as a pure driver’s car: Tactile, analog, and deeply mechanical, including the shift lever with an exposed titanium linkage, a squarish shift knob with inset glass, and a six-speed gear pattern etched on top. McLaren said the shifter’s throws aim for maximum feel. Extra nostalgic feels come from a “Speedy Kiwi” shield logo on the B-pillars. It’s the brand’s famous but long-retired race signature, a graphic of that flightless bird. The same logo is etched onto the fuel-filler cap. Furthering the mechanical character is hydraulic steering, tactile switchgear, and machined details inspired by the original M6GT. Knurled analog switches take place of pride over a surfeit of screens. A gauge cluster integrated atop the steering wheel looks positively weapons-grade, a single rectangular screen bookended by a chunky pair of machined-metal rocker switches. Those rockers let drivers control suspension and performance settings without taking their hands off the flat-bottomed steering wheel. Driver instruments are one area where McLaren chose digital over analog, with a claim to retaining “the clarity and emotional appeal of the original.” Collins called the car “symbolic of the bold, provocative and hugely exciting future we are preparing to realize.” Company executives weren’t ready to say if that future will officially include an SUV of the type that has boosted the bottom line for rivals such as Aston Martin, Lamborghini, and Ferrari. McLaren’s latent rediscovery of its founder’s stillborn street car may suggest it has taken a longstanding criticism to heart: That today’s McLarens, with their shared components and philosophies—a carbon-fiber tub and function above all—are sometimes difficult to tell apart, even when they’re not traveling at blurry speeds. In July, the company unveiled a limited-production 788 HS, billed as the “definitive final chapter” for a V-8 platform that began with the 720S and proceeded through the 765LT and 750S. The brand began connecting dots to its history when it showed a reproduction of that original M6GT, created by McLaren Special Operations, at the Goodwood Festival of Speed this summer, with a fiberglass body and Chevy small-block V-8. That painstaking reproduction, via original body molds, archival drawings, and remade parts, was also present at the company’s car week “House of McLaren” in Carmel, California. The reborn M6GT was joined by a W1 hypercar and a 788HS Coupe and Spyder. Capping things off was a MCL-HY GTS, the new Le Mans Hypercar racer set to compete in the 2027 FIA World Endurance Championship. But it’s the McL 6GT, coming in 2028, that may offer the clearest showroom picture of McLaren’s ability to turn things around.
