title: Arsenal v Man City: What is the FA Community Shield? - Premier League
content: All you need to know about the traditional curtain-raiser to the top-flight season The prelude to the 2026/27 Premier League season takes place on Sunday 16 August as Arsenal and Manchester City lock horns in the 2026 FA Community Shield. The Community Shield was founded in 1908, and is an annual match contested between the Premier League champions and the winners of the FA Cup. If the same team wins both trophies, then the Premier League runners’ up faces the title winners. The 2025 FA Cup victors Crystal Palace are the current holders, having defeated 2024/25 Premier League champions Liverpool last August, winning 3-2 on penalties after a 2-2 draw in regulation time. This year, Premier League champions Arsenal take on Man City, who defeated Chelsea in the FA Cup final at Wembley Stadium in May to win the trophy for the eighth time in their history. It’ll mark the first meeting between last season's title rivals since City’s 2-1 Premier League win over Arsenal in April. The last time the two teams faced off in cup competition, City emerged victorious in the 2026 EFL Cup final. A second-half double from Nico O’Reilly saw the Manchester giants claim a 2-0 win over Arsenal. The clubs last faced each other in the Community Shield in 2023, with Arsenal winning 4-1 on penalties after a 1-1 draw in normal time. The winning side claim the first major piece of domestic silverware of the season. Rather than handed a trophy per se, the winner of the Community Shield is presented with a "shield". The base is fitted with individually engraved plates that feature the names of past winners and the years they won. Community Shield success should set a team up for a successful campaign, right? Well, not necessarily. History suggests that winning the Community Shield can be more of a curse rather than a blessing. Only once in the last 16 years have a team gone on to claim a Community Shield and Premier League double, Man City achieving the feat in 2018/19. Remarkably, it has only been done eight times since the Premier League’s inception in 1992. Furthermore, the losing team in the Community Shield have gone on to claim the Premier League title more times (10) than the winner (eight) since 1992. Since 1974, the Community Shield had been played at Wembley rather than a number of guest venues across the country, as was the case in earlier editions. Between 2001 and 2006, the game was switched to the Principality Stadium, formerly known as the Millennium Stadium, in Cardiff as Wembley underwent renovations. And only twice since 2007 has the match been played away from Wembley. In 2012, Villa Park, home of Aston Villa, hosted the Community Shield contest between Man City and Chelsea due to the Olympic Games held in London. And in 2022, Wembley hosted the Women’s European Championship final, meaning the clash between Man City and Liverpool took place at Leicester City’s home ground, the King Power Stadium. For the first time in 20 years, the Community Shield will be contested in Cardiff. That’s because of music artist The Weeknd’s "After Hours Til Dawn" tour taking place on the same day at the stadium, which means the Community Shield will be played away from Wembley for only the third time since it reopened in 2007. title: Coach V’s Corner: I’ve Never Seen a Woodchuck - Post Independent
content: It has to be well over 30 years now that I received a call late on an August Friday night from my friend and running buddy Bob Willey. He wanted to know if I would join him the following morning for a new 5-mile race at Rifle Falls State Park called the Cheatin’ Woodchuck Chase. After immediately declining his invite, I wondered out loud if race directors would release a large group of varmints in the park, with adult human varmints in hot pursuit. Whoever catches the first one wins, or loses, depending on the temperament of that particular woodchuck. It seemed silly. After much cajoling from Willey, with a few guilt trips thrown in for good measure, I agreed to go on what was sure to be a foolhardy adventure. An adventure it turned out to be, indeed. After picking me up bright and early, Willey’s dilapidated old Audi decided to start shaking and belching smoke on Interstate 70 just west of New Castle. When the rattling and rusty old relic finally made it clear of traffic and safely to the side of the road, all I could think of to say was, “Well, at least we weren’t in an airplane!” With hopes of chasing elusive woodchucks now completely dashed, Willey and I got on U.S. 6 and 24 and jogged back to New Castle, stopping at Mattivi’s gas station. As luck would have it, a tow truck and a driver were right there on site. I had never ridden in one, but it was quite a treat hitching up the car and getting a tow back to Glenwood Springs in the big rig, with Willey giving the driver an earful about our misbegotten morning the entire way. Not to be denied, the following year, we jumped into a much more reliable vehicle and made it to the race. In the many years that have followed our abbreviated initial attempt, I have made it to more Woodchuck Chases than I can count, but I have yet to see an actual woodchuck! I’ll give it another shot this year on Saturday, Aug. 22. Sponsored once again by Rifle Recreation, the race is now a 5K and will begin and end near the Rifle State Fish Hatchery. The format is a little different this year, with runners going up the road from the hatchery for 1.55 miles and then retracing their steps back down. Start time is 9 a.m., and full details can be found at the EcoPoint Race Series on the Rifle Recreation website. Don’t forget about Saturday’s Dog Day 5K at Two Rivers Park in Glenwood Springs. The Aug. 15 run starts and finishes near the bandshell and is out and back on the Rio Grande Trail. The start time is 9 a.m., and all proceeds will benefit Colorado Animal Rescue. When I saw that Roaring Fork High School would once again field a varsity football team at the 1A level, I was reminded of all the great rivalry games between the Rams and the Glenwood Demons back when I was in high school in the late 1970s. The game between the two undefeated Northwestern League leaders in the late fall of 1978 is still the best game, with the biggest crowd I have ever witnessed at Glenwood’s stadium. It wasn’t called Stubler Memorial Field at the time because Coach Stubler was still a legend in the making as one of the assistant football coaches for the Demons. Glenwood and coach Don Miller went on to win that hard-fought game against the Rams and capture the 2A state championship a few months later on a snowy December Saturday in Glenwood Springs that was better suited for penguins than football players and fans. I wish Coach John Nielsen and the Rams the very best of luck this fall. The first game is at home in Carbondale on Friday night, Aug. 21, against Gunnison, with a 7 p.m. kickoff. I will get up to Carbondale for a few games and also catch some of the Demons this fall at what is now Stubler Memorial Field. title: Instant takeaways from Colts preseason performance v. Patriots - Yahoo Sports
content: The Indianapolis Colts fell by a score of X to X to the New England Patriots in their preseason opener. But this time of the year isn't about wins and losses. In the preseason, individual performances often take priority, with playing time, roles, and roster spots up for grabs. With the clock now at triple zeros, here are our instant takeaways from what took place. - Anthony Richardson was 11-for-14 passing for 145 yards -- although his performance was more up and down than the stat line shows. That said, the passing game generated four plays of at least 16 yards and Richardson's impact with the ball in his hands was felt, as he rushed for 54 yards and a score. He did have an interception, but it went through Coleman Owen's hands. - Riley Leonard's performance was more inconsistent. He was 10-for-20 passing for 89 yards with an interception that was a bad decision and a bad throw. He seemed to struggle to find a rhythm. - Linebacker is a question mark, but the backups -- who saw starting snaps in this game -- Jaylon Carlies, Austin Ajiake, and Bryce Boettcher performed well. - On the flip side, it was very up and down for the backup cornerbacks. Mekhi Blackmon was penalized twice, and Johnathan Edwards had a rough showing. - That said, Edwards will be a very good special teams player for the Colts. - Rookie defensive end George Gumbs showcased his potential, logging a sack and a tackle for loss. Fellow rookie Caden Curry had a good night as well. - Coleman Owen was quite impressive as a return man. When it comes to the final roster spot at wide receiver, that role could be the differentiator between Owen, Deion Burks, and Anthony Gould. - Jaylahn Tuimoloau got the start and went against backup tackles, but it was a quiet night for him. - Ulysses Bentley's ability to impact the passing game can help him make a roster push. DJ Giddens remains sidelined, and the Colts could use that pass-catching element. - Of note, Dalton Tucker got the starting center reps with Tanor Bortolini not playing. Jalen Travis was at right tackle and Blake Freeland at left tackle. - Jonathan Owens is going to be an important special teams player this season. - Blake Grupe entered the game with the advantage over Spencer Shrader, but Grupe was 0/1 kicking, while Shrader was 2/2, which included making a 61-yarder late to tie the game. - Tight end Will Mallory has put together some good practices as of late and continued that performance in this game. Shane Steichen needs to get him more opportunities this season. This article originally appeared on Colts Wire: Instant takeaways from Colts preseason performance v. Patriots

title: Recapping Anthony Richardson's performance in Colts v. Patriots - Yahoo Sports
content: Anthony Richardson played the entire first half in the Indianapolis Colts' preseason opener against the New England Patriots, and he put together what may have been his best performance of training camp. Richardson finished the first half by completing 11-of-14 passes for 145 yards. Under Richardson, the Colts' offense was able to generate several chunk plays, with four players recording one reception of at least 16 yards. We also saw Richardson's ability to impact the game with the ball in his hands, rushing for 53 yards on six attempts with a touchdown. In the final minutes of the first half, Richardson led a scoring drive and put the Colts in field goal range at the end of half. That said, there were ups and downs as well. While Richardson's interception should have instead been a reception by Coleman Owen, the pass was slightly off target and into tight coverage. He also fumbled once as a ball carrier. But overall, a promising performance for the fourth-year quarterback who is competing with Riley Leonard for the backup role. Now, the biggest thing for Richardson will be maintaining this consistency moving forward. This article originally appeared on Colts Wire: Recapping Anthony Richardson's performance in Colts v. title: Once upon a time: storytelling in Learning Resources v. Trump - SCOTUSblog
content: Every fall, with each new class of 1Ls, we legal writing teachers undertake a strange job. We spend an entire year trying to get students to not write like lawyers, a notoriously dreadful category of writers. In pursuit of that goal, we often target the bad qualities like jargon, legalese, word-wasting phrases, and other legal idiosyncrasies. But I think we’d get better results if we started with what makes any writing “good” – whether it is written by lawyers or by actual humans. As evidence, I would point to the Supreme Court’s best writers, who deploy tactics often taught (and missed) in a good English composition class. Take Chief Justice John Roberts as an example. Flash back to November 2025: if you’re Roberts, you’ve got a problem – or at least a challenge. You’ve just assigned yourself the majority opinion in Learning Resources v. Trump. Now you must convince readers inside and outside the court that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act provides no authority for the one policy most important to this president: tariffs. Never mind that the solicitor general has warned that your decision will provoke another Great Depression. Never mind that the outcome depends upon Talmudic esoterica unfamiliar to a politicized public – things like separation of powers, textualism, and the major questions doctrine. Beyond all that, you must communicate dreadful source material, especially to non-legal readers. Those readers must learn something of IEEPA itself, which clocks in at around 2,000 words of abstract text. Then, they need the content of the president’s orders, which add almost 12,000 words, even without the appendices. Roberts solves this problem by meeting the expectations of the ordinary, English-language reader. Apart from citations, he tells a 422-word story, and he does it with a tactic any writer can emulate: He uses actors as the subjects of most of his sentences. In a conflict over presidential power, Roberts makes the president the main character in a story, both in setting out IEEPA’s requirements and in summarizing the president’s orders. After an initial topic sentence about IEEPA, he puts the president – rather than the statute – in the subject position. He writes that, to satisfy IEEPA, “the President must identify” a threat. Then, “he must declare” an emergency. Then “he” may “regulate [. . . 16 words later . . .] importation.” Turning to the facts, the chief keeps the president – rather than his orders – in the spotlight. He practically ties the president to a chair at center stage. In the narrative, “President Trump sought” to address two, specific threats (“The first was the influx of illegal drugs from Canada, Mexico, and China,” and “[t]he second was ‘large and persistent’ trade deficits.”). Roberts writes that the “President determined” the threats were serious. “He invoked” his power under IEEPA. As required by the statute, “President Trump declared” the requisite emergency. “He then imposed” tariffs, which “the President” later changed when “he increased” or “he removed” tariffs. Later, “the President . . . shifted . . . goods into and out of” the tariff regime. Indeed, in all the sentences he wrote for Section I.A of the opinion, the chief used an actor as the subject in all but five. In making that choice, the chief is not employing some tactic unique to “legal” writing, separate from ordinary English prose. Your old English composition teacher has long known the power of storytelling language. One such teacher, Joseph Willams, changed the way I wrote as a lawyer, and I love the way he put it. In the book Style: Lessons in Clarity and Grace, he focuses on what every reader needs from a writer. While readers look for action in the verbs, “they want characters as subjects even more.” You erect tripping hazards for your reader when, “for no good reason,” you “fail to name characters in subjects, or worse, delete them entirely.” Unfortunately, most lawyers don’t write this way. Most lawyers – even great ones – write more like the Congressional Research Service. In its September 2025 report on IEEPA, CRS covers essentially the same ground as the chief’s 422-word story. But instead of a story, CRS offers up a report filled with tripping hazards. It force-feeds the reader five dense pages (10–14) of abstract prose, replete with footnotes. Where Roberts describes IEEPA by focusing on the president, CRS hangs a 56-word sentence on “IEEPA empowers.” Readers must then swallow a 50-word sentence hung on “statute provides.” And the public is reminded that each “new threat . . . requires” certain actions by the president. The coup de grace? CRS treats readers to a dreadful block quote of IEEPA’s central provisions. To be sure, the president does appear in the paragraphs discussing the tariff orders. But if Roberts ties the president to a chair, CRS permits him to wander on and off stage. In the president’s absence, readers must content themselves with massive sentences about the “January Proclamation” or the “February Executive Orders.” Again, rather than a story, the reader must shoulder a bureaucratic tome – scrupulously accurate, no doubt, but abstract enough and long enough to avoid being read at all. The chief, in contrast, uses storytelling both to be read and to be understood, all while setting up his version of the question. Remember the story: The president issued barely related tariffs that swallowed the entire economy, then he changed them at random. But Congress wrote, “regulate . . . [yadda, yadda, yadda] . . . importation.” Based on this language, can a president really set tariffs “on imports from any country, of any product, at any rate, for any amount of time”? So, how to write like the chief rather than like a lawyer? Prefer actors as subjects rather than concepts or abstractions like proclamations, orders, tariffs, separation of powers, or the major questions doctrine. Of course, “prefer” means you’ll occasionally discover “good reason” to abandon this approach, but not nearly as often as you think. For the moment, create drafts like you always do, then build in storytelling when you line edit. In the end, good legal writers do the same things as good writers in any field. Good writers tell stories where characters do things. And here, the president was doing things, but without a permission slip from congress. title: BTS Member V Reveals Hearing-Loss Issues Amid World Tour - Rolling Stone
content: BTS’ V revealed Wednesday that he has been suffering from hearing loss for nearly two-and-a-half years, with one ear functioning at roughly one-third of the other. The singer born Kim Tae-hyung disclosed his condition for the first time Wednesday during a livestream to fans: “If the hearing in my left ear is at 100, it’s only about 30 in my right.” V didn’t detail the cause of the issue. V’s hearing issues became worse while he was serving his mandatory military service, and at first he ignored the issue, determining it to be “a matter of mental strength,” the BBC reports. As the condition progressed, however, V eventually looped in doctors, and the singer is now receiving medication and going to the hospital regularly to battle the condition. V isn’t the only BTS member dealing with health issues as the group continues its Arirang world tour, which concluded its Baltimore dates on Wednesday: Jungkook also revealed during the livestream that he’s been dealing with a shin injury that is “on the verge of developing a stress fracture,” but he’ll continue to perform through the injury. “There’s a lot of inflammation in my shin, and I think there’s some microdamage to the bone,” Jungkook, who has performed seated at a few BTS shows this tour, said. “I’ll be careful with myself so I can finish this tour properly.” The Arirang world tour only has four more stops in North America — Arlington, Texas, Toronto, Chicago, and a four-night stand at Los Angeles’ SoFi Stadium — before the trek moves to South America, the South Pacific, Australia, and Hong Kong.
